options.text: Have the report subagent append a line to each report stating that its citations were verified
options.explanation: A statement written by the model is not verification and would be false in exactly the runs that skipped the check.

options.text: Add a hook blocking publish_report until a passing verify_citations result exists for that run

explanation: Correct: D. When compliance must be deterministic, a programmatic prerequisite gate beats prompt guidance, which keeps a non-zero failure rate (9 of 400 here). A hook that refuses publish_report until verification has passed guarantees the order. Why not the others: A and B are still prompt guidance; C asserts verification without performing it.

prompt: Each analysis run is supplied with 300 to 600 internal documents hosted behind a remote custom MCP server. Traces show the document analysis subagent spending its first 20 to 30 tool calls on `search_documents` with guessed keywords, just to learn what the corpus contains. What change to the MCP server most directly cuts this?

options.text: Add a dump_corpus tool that returns the full text of each document in one response for the subagent to scan
options.explanation: Hundreds of full documents in one tool result would flood the subagent's context and bury the relevant material.

options.text: Expose the corpus catalog (titles, types, dates, section outline) as an MCP resource the subagent reads
Raise search_documents' result limit from 10 to 100 hits so each guessed query returns far more matches
options.explanation: Bigger result pages make each blind query noisier and costlier; the subagent still has to guess what to search for.

options.text: Have the coordinator pass the corpus's folder path so the subagent can Glob the directory structure itself
options.explanation: The documents live behind a remote MCP server, not on the agent's filesystem, so built-in Glob cannot reach them.

explanation: Correct: B. MCP resources expose content catalogs such as document hierarchies, giving the agent a map of what exists and cutting exploratory tool calls. Why not the others: A floods context with full text; C enlarges each blind search instead of removing the need for it; D assumes local file access to a corpus that sits behind a remote server.

prompt: The web search subagent has clear, detailed descriptions for `search_news` and `search_scholarly`, and in isolated tests it picks correctly. In production it calls `search_news` for most academic questions. Its system prompt, carried over from an early prototype, includes: "For any question about recent findings, start with search_news." What should be done?

options.text: Expand search_scholarly's description with many more example queries so it outweighs the other tool
options.explanation: The descriptions already work in isolation; the system-prompt instruction is what overrides them, and it would remain.

options.text: Force tool_choice to search_scholarly whenever a question contains the word study or journal
options.explanation: Keyword routing in application code is brittle and misses academic questions phrased without those words.

options.text: Merge both into one search tool with a source parameter so the subagent cannot choose wrongly
options.explanation: The prompt would bias the source parameter the same way, and merging discards two well-scoped tools.

options.text: Review the system prompt and remove or reword the line steering recent-findings questions to news

explanation: Correct: D. Keyword-sensitive wording in a system prompt can override good tool descriptions; academic questions often mention recent findings, so the prototype line pushes them to search_news. Removing or rewording it fixes the cause. Why not the others: A strengthens descriptions that already work; B adds brittle keyword routing; C moves the same bias into a parameter.

prompt: Analysts spot-check citations: across 2,000 sampled claims, 97% are supported by the cited source. Management proposes cutting human citation review to 1% of reports. Nobody has yet broken the results down by source type (web pages, born-digital PDFs, scanned archives). What should happen before review is reduced?

options.text: Validate accuracy per source type and keep stratified random sampling of high-confidence claims
Cut review to 1% now, since a 97% aggregate over 2,000 claims is strong enough evidence on its own
options.explanation: An aggregate can hide a weak segment, such as scanned archives, whose error rate is far higher than the average.

options.text: Have the synthesis subagent self-report confidence and skip human review when the score exceeds 0.9
options.explanation: Uncalibrated self-reported confidence is a poor routing signal; it must be calibrated on labelled data first.

options.text: Focus the remaining human review on the reports that analysts rate as most important to the business
options.explanation: Business importance says nothing about where citation errors cluster, so weak source types stay unmeasured.

explanation: Correct: A. Aggregate accuracy can hide weak document types or fields, so accuracy should be validated per segment before reducing review, and stratified random sampling of high-confidence output keeps measuring error and surfacing new failure patterns. Why not the others: B trusts the aggregate; C routes on uncalibrated confidence; D samples by importance rather than by error risk.

prompt: The system handles two kinds of work. Weekly competitor briefs cover the same five aspects each time: pricing, launches, hiring, filings and press. Ad-hoc investigations, such as "why did our churn spike in Brazil last quarter?", often turn up leads midway that change what should be researched next. Which design fits?

options.text: A fixed pipeline for the briefs, and adaptive decomposition revised as findings arrive for investigations
Adaptive decomposition for both, since letting the coordinator replan freely gives the best result on any task
options.explanation: For a predictable, repeated structure, a fixed pipeline is cheaper and more consistent; replanning adds variance for no gain.

options.text: A fixed pipeline for both, with the investigation pipeline extended to cover each plausible cause up front
options.explanation: Open-ended investigations cannot enumerate causes in advance; a fixed plan cannot follow leads that appear midway.

options.text: Adaptive decomposition for the briefs and a fixed pipeline for investigations, so costs stay predictable
options.explanation: This reverses the fit: the predictable task gets variable planning and the open-ended one gets a rigid script.

explanation: Correct: A. Fixed sequential pipelines (prompt chaining) suit predictable multi-aspect work like a standing brief, while open-ended investigations need dynamic decomposition that adapts as findings emerge. Why not the others: B gives up the consistency of a pipeline where structure is known; C forces a rigid plan on open-ended work; D swaps the two.

prompt: The team wants a shared `.mcp.json` in the repository that configures the paid search provider's MCP server for each developer working on the research system. The server needs an API key, and each developer has a personal one. How should the key be supplied?

options.text: Reference it in .mcp.json as ${SEARCH_API_KEY} and have each developer set that variable in their environment
Commit one shared team key in .mcp.json, since the repository is private and access to it is already controlled
options.explanation: Secrets committed to version control leak through clones, forks and history, and a shared key cannot be traced or revoked per person.

options.text: Keep the server out of .mcp.json, and have each developer add it to ~/.claude.json with their key and settings
options.explanation: User scope suits personal or experimental servers; it gives up the shared, versioned configuration the team asked for.

options.text: Put the key in the project's CLAUDE.md so that the agent can read it at startup and pass it to the MCP server
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is committed instructions for the model, not a secret store or a source of server configuration.

explanation: Correct: A. Project-scoped .mcp.json is shared through version control, and environment variable expansion such as ${SEARCH_API_KEY} lets each developer supply a personal key without committing secrets. Why not the others: B commits a secret; C abandons the shared project configuration; D puts a secret into a committed instruction file the server does not read.

prompt: The web search subagent has a generic `fetch_url` tool. An audit found it following links to internal admin URLs that appeared inside scraped pages, and pulling 40 MB dataset files whose contents blew through its context. How should the tool be redesigned?

options.text: Replace fetch_url with load_document, which checks URLs against allowed domains and caps content size
Keep fetch_url but add a system-prompt warning against fetching internal hosts or files that look very large
options.explanation: A prompt warning is probabilistic, and links planted in scraped pages are exactly where the model may be misled.

options.text: Keep fetch_url and add a PostToolUse hook that truncates each fetched response to its first 2,000 characters
options.explanation: Truncating after the call limits context use but the internal request has already been made; it does not stop the bad fetch.

options.text: Move fetch_url to the coordinator so that each fetch is decided centrally rather than by the search subagent
options.explanation: The same unconstrained tool now bloats the coordinator's context, and nothing validates the URLs it is given.

explanation: Correct: A. Replacing a generic tool with a constrained one, such as load_document that validates URLs and bounds what it returns, builds the limits into the tool itself. Why not the others: B leaves safety to the prompt; C acts after the internal request has already gone out; D moves the unconstrained tool and its context cost to the coordinator.

prompt: An analyst paused a named session on lithium prices on Friday. By Monday, two of the five supplier sites it had scraped had published new quarterly data, and she had decided to narrow the question to South America. Most of the session's earlier tool results are now stale or out of scope. How should work continue?

options.text: Start a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of still-valid findings and the narrowed question
Run --resume with the session name and tell it the question has narrowed, keeping its earlier tool results
options.explanation: Resuming suits context that is mostly still valid; here most tool results are stale or off-scope and would mislead the work.

options.text: Resume the session and have it re-fetch the two changed sites, keeping the rest of its context as it was
options.explanation: Targeted re-analysis fits when little has changed; it leaves the out-of-scope material for the other regions in context.

options.text: Fork the Friday session with fork_session so the new direction branches off from the existing baseline
options.explanation: Forking copies the stale baseline into the new branch; it is for comparing approaches from a baseline that is still valid.

explanation: Correct: A. Resume when prior context is mostly valid; when most tool results are stale or out of scope, a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of what still holds is more reliable. Why not the others: B and C carry the stale and off-scope results forward; D branches from that same outdated baseline.

prompt: The document analysis subagent receives 35 supplied contracts in one request and is asked to find clauses that conflict across them. It reports detailed findings for the first few and last few contracts but misses obvious conflicts involving contracts from the middle of the set. Which restructuring addresses this?

options.text: Raise the subagent's max_tokens so it has room to write findings for each of the 35 contracts in one reply
options.explanation: The problem is attention spread across a huge input, not output space; a longer reply does not make the middle contracts read better.

options.text: Sort the contracts by length so the shortest ones sit in the middle, where attention tends to be weakest
options.explanation: Reordering moves which contracts get neglected rather than fixing the dilution of attention across 35 documents.

options.text: Ask the subagent to be thorough and to read the full set twice before it reports conflicting clauses
options.explanation: An exhortation to be thorough does not change how attention is spread over one very large input.

options.text: Run a per-contract pass that extracts key clauses, then a separate cross-contract pass comparing them

explanation: Correct: D. Splitting the work into focused per-document passes plus a cross-document integration pass avoids the attention dilution of one huge input, and the comparison then runs over compact extractions. Why not the others: A adds output room for an input problem; B reshuffles which contracts are neglected; C relies on an instruction that does not change how attention is spread.

prompt: After two weeks of production runs you notice the synthesis subagent's briefings regularly omit findings from the academic-research subagent. Inspecting the transcripts: each research subagent dumps 8–15 paper abstracts (often 500+ tokens each) into its tool-call results as part of returning its findings to the coordinator. By the time the synthesis subagent runs, its context window contains ~40 abstracts plus the original instructions, and it appears to lose track of earlier material. What is the most appropriate **architectural** fix?

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` on the synthesis subagent so that its briefing has enough room to mention every finding it receives
options.explanation: Works on the output side. A longer briefing does not help a model that has lost track of findings buried in its input.

options.text: Have each research subagent return a short structured summary (key findings, sources with URLs) and save full abstracts to files the synthesis step can read on demand
Move the synthesis subagent to a larger model with a longer context window, so that all forty abstracts fit comfortably
options.explanation: A model swap, not an architectural fix: the design still grows the synthesis context without bound, and middle material still gets lost.

options.text: Add a hook that compacts the conversation automatically whenever the running token count passes 100,000 tokens
options.explanation: Compaction is lossy and indiscriminate; it may summarise away exactly the findings that were being dropped.

explanation: Correct: B. Subagents exist to do verbose work in their own context and hand back only what the next step needs. Returning raw abstracts moves the bloat into the coordinator and synthesis contexts, where findings in the middle get lost; compact structured summaries with sources, plus detail available on demand, keep every finding visible. Why not the others: A enlarges the output, not the model's grip on its input; C keeps an unbounded design on a bigger model; D throws information away indiscriminately.

prompt:
The news-research subagent is meant to read web sources only. In practice you discover it occasionally creates a file `notes.md` in the project root with scratch notes, which then leak into git commits. Its current definition is:

```markdown
---
name: news-researcher
description: Investigates recent news on the topic
tools: Read, Write, Edit, WebFetch, WebSearch
---

You research recent news on a given topic and return a summary...
```

What is the simplest durable fix?

options.text: Append to the subagent's prompt body: "Never call Write or Edit. Return your notes inline in your reply only."
options.explanation: A prompt instruction is followed most of the time, not every time; the tools remain available to call.

options.text: Drop `Write` and `Edit` from the `tools:` frontmatter, leaving only `Read, WebFetch, WebSearch`
Set `permissionMode: plan` on the subagent so that it cannot modify any files on disk
options.explanation: Plan mode is meant for a plan-then-approve workflow, not for permanently scoping a worker's tools.

options.text: Add a `PreToolUse` hook for this subagent that rejects every `Write` or `Edit` call it makes
options.explanation: Works, but enforces at runtime what the subagent definition can express declaratively in one line.

explanation: Correct: B. The `tools` field in a subagent definition is the declarative way to scope what it can do: list only the tools the role needs and the others cannot be called at all. Why not the others: A relies on the model obeying a prohibition; C borrows a mode built for a different workflow; D adds runtime machinery for what is a static allowlist.

prompt: An engineer asks the assistant: "Add meaningful unit tests to the billing-reconciler service." The service is 14 years old, spans 380 Python files and has almost no tests. How should the assistant approach this open-ended request? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run a fixed four-step chain on each file (read, summarise, write tests, lint), working through all 380 files alphabetically.
options.explanation: A fixed per-file pipeline suits predictable reviews, not open-ended work. It never prioritises, so effort goes to trivial files as much as critical ones.

options.text: Map the module structure and dependencies first, then pick out high-impact areas such as money-handling paths to test first.
Draft a prioritised test plan and revise it as findings emerge, for example when a module turns out to be dead code.
Ask for tests covering the whole service in one request so the model sees every file at once and keeps a single style.
options.explanation: Loading 380 files into one request dilutes attention and overflows useful context; the open-ended task needs mapping and an adaptive plan instead.

options.text: Begin with the files that have the most lines, since larger files tend to hold the most defects worth covering by tests.
options.explanation: File size is a crude proxy. High impact comes from what the code does (money paths, entry points), which only a structural map reveals.

explanation: Correct: B and C. Open-ended tasks like adding tests to a legacy codebase call for dynamic decomposition: map the structure, find the high-impact areas, then follow a prioritised plan that adapts as you learn. Why not the others: A applies a fixed pipeline with no prioritisation; D floods one request and dilutes attention; E swaps impact analysis for a line-count heuristic.

prompt: The team packages a `legacy-audit` skill that fires dozens of Grep and Read calls over an old service and prints long intermediate listings. Engineers complain the listings flood their main conversation, and the security lead wants the audit to be unable to change files. Which TWO frontmatter settings in its SKILL.md address this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: context: fork, so the audit runs in an isolated sub-agent context and only its result comes back to the main session
argument-hint: read-only, so Claude is reminded throughout the run that it must not modify any files
options.explanation: argument-hint prompts the user for parameters when the skill is invoked; it does not restrict what tools the skill can use.

options.text: Moving the skill text into the project CLAUDE.md so it is loaded into every session from the very start
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is always loaded and meant for universal standards. It neither isolates verbose output nor restricts tools, and it costs context in every session.

options.text: allowed-tools listing just Read, Grep and Glob, so the skill cannot edit files or run shell commands while active
Placing the skill under ~/.claude/skills/ so that its verbose output stays in a personal context rather than the shared one
options.explanation: The skill's location decides who has it (personal vs shared), not whether its output is isolated from the main conversation.

explanation: Correct: A and D. context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so verbose output does not pollute the main session, and allowed-tools restricts the tools available while the skill runs. Why not the others: B misuses argument-hint, which only prompts for parameters; C makes the workflow always-loaded without isolation or restriction; E changes who can use the skill, not where its output goes.

prompt: Priya's Claude Code sessions in the `invoicing` repo consistently route HTTP calls through the internal `corehttp` wrapper. A new hire on the same repo and branch gets code that calls `requests` directly. The repository's CLAUDE.md says nothing about HTTP clients, and running /memory on the two laptops lists different files. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: The new hire runs an older Claude Code release; upgrading it lets the project CLAUDE.md be parsed the same way.
options.explanation: Both use the same project CLAUDE.md, which lacks the rule entirely. A version difference cannot add an instruction that is not there.

options.text: Commit a copy of Priya's .claude/settings.json so the new hire inherits the same set of coding instructions.
options.explanation: settings.json holds permissions and configuration, not memory instructions. The rule is in a CLAUDE.md file, not settings.

options.text: Ask the new hire to paste the rule at the start of each session, since memory files load just for their author.
options.explanation: Project memory files load for anyone in the repo. Pasting the rule each session is fragile and treats the symptom, not the misplaced file.

options.text: The rule sits in Priya's user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md; move it to the project CLAUDE.md in the repo.

explanation: Correct: D. The user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md applies only to that user and is not shared through version control; /memory showing different loaded files confirms it. Team conventions belong in the project CLAUDE.md. Why not the others: A blames a version difference for a missing rule; B confuses settings with memory; C wrongly claims project memory is per-author and relies on manual pasting.

prompt: Two hours into exploring a payments monolith, the assistant's answers drift. Early on it named the `LedgerGateway` class as the write path; now it says "this kind of system typically uses a repository layer" and contradicts an answer from forty minutes ago. The engineer still has a day of exploration ahead. What change best fixes this?

options.text: Raise max_tokens on each request so responses have room to cite the classes found earlier in full detail.
options.explanation: max_tokens caps output length. The problem is degraded recall over a long, cluttered context, which a larger output budget does not touch.

options.text: Restart in a new session and redo the same exploration with identical prompts, only this time more carefully.
options.explanation: Repeating the same process rebuilds the same cluttered context and the drift returns; nothing persists findings or isolates verbose output.

options.text: Keep key findings in a scratchpad file as they emerge, push verbose searches to subagents, and reread it.
Add a system-prompt line saying it must always name specific classes and must not describe typical patterns.
options.explanation: An instruction cannot restore facts the model is losing track of in an overloaded context. Persisted findings and isolated exploration can.

explanation: Correct: C. Long exploration sessions degrade into generic "typical pattern" answers. A scratchpad file persists key findings outside the conversation, and subagents keep verbose discovery output out of the main context. Why not the others: A changes output length, not recall; B rebuilds the same problem; D asks for behaviour the degraded context cannot support.

prompt: The assistant's loop ends when the latest assistant text contains phrases like "I'm done" or "task complete". Logs show two failures: some runs stop while a tool_use block is still waiting to be executed, and others keep looping after the model has clearly finished. How should the loop decide whether to continue?

options.text: Branch on stop_reason: run the tools and append each tool_result when it is "tool_use"; exit on "end_turn".
Extend the phrase list with more completion wordings and lowercase the text before matching to reduce misses.
options.explanation: Parsing natural language for termination is the anti-pattern itself. More phrases still miss wordings and still ignore pending tool calls.

options.text: Cap the loop at 10 iterations and treat reaching that cap as the normal signal that the work has finished.
options.explanation: An iteration cap can be a safety net, but as the primary stop it cuts off long tasks and wastes calls on short ones.

options.text: Ask the model to end each final answer with a DONE token and stop the loop as soon as that token shows up.
options.explanation: This is still text parsing: the token can appear alongside a tool_use request or be omitted. stop_reason already signals this reliably.

explanation: Correct: A. The agentic loop inspects stop_reason: "tool_use" means execute the requested tools, append the results and call again; "end_turn" means the model is finished. Why not the others: B and D keep parsing assistant text to decide termination, a named anti-pattern; C makes an arbitrary iteration cap the primary stopping rule.

prompt: Yesterday an engineer spent three hours in a named session, `auth-map`, tracing how the legacy auth module issues tokens. Overnight a teammate merged a refactor that renamed or split about half of that module's files. The engineer wants to continue the investigation this morning. What should they do?

options.text: Run --resume auth-map and keep asking questions; the model will notice the renamed files by itself as it goes.
options.explanation: Resuming carries yesterday's tool results, half of which now describe files that no longer exist. The model will reason from stale reads.

options.text: Resume the session and paste the full merge diff so the model can reconcile every old tool result on its own.
options.explanation: Naming changed files works when most prior context is still valid. Here half the reads are stale, and a huge diff adds clutter rather than clarity.

options.text: Start a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of yesterday's findings, then re-read changed files.
Use fork_session on yesterday's session so the stale and the current views of the module sit side by side.
options.explanation: Forking branches from a shared baseline to compare approaches. Both branches would still carry the stale tool results.

explanation: Correct: C. When much of the prior context is stale, a fresh session with a structured summary beats resuming with outdated tool results; resume (telling the session which files changed) only when prior context is mostly valid. Why not the others: A trusts the model to notice staleness; B resumes despite half the context being invalid; D misuses fork_session, which is for comparing approaches.

prompt: The assistant's coordinator answers "explain this legacy code" questions by running four subagents in sequence: dependency graph, git history, docs lookup and summary writer. A question like "what does `parse_iso` in util/dates.py return?" takes 90 seconds because all four run every time. What is the best change?

options.text: Merge the four subagents into one generalist with every tool, so a single call covers any kind of question.
options.explanation: A generalist with every tool loses focused context and degrades tool selection; the real issue is invoking work a question does not need.

options.text: Have the coordinator gauge complexity and invoke only the subagents each question needs, e.g. one reader.
Give the four subagents one shared conversation history so each can skip work another has already done.
options.explanation: Subagents are designed with isolated context. Sharing history removes that isolation and still runs all four for a one-line question.

options.text: Have each subagent call the next one directly when it needs input, removing the coordinator round-trips.
options.explanation: Routing through the coordinator keeps observability and consistent error handling. Direct chaining still runs the full pipeline.

explanation: Correct: B. In hub-and-spoke designs the coordinator picks which subagents to invoke based on query complexity rather than always running the full pipeline. Why not the others: A trades focused roles for one overloaded agent; C breaks subagent context isolation without skipping work; D bypasses the coordinator, losing observability and error handling.

prompt: The docs server exposes `find_info` ("Finds information") and the issue tracker exposes `lookup` ("Looks up information"). Asked "how do I configure the retry policy in the ingest service?", the assistant queries the issue tracker, returns three stale bug threads and misses the design doc that answers it. What fix addresses the root cause?

options.text: Rewrite both descriptions with inputs, example queries, boundaries (design docs vs bugs) and when to use each.
Add a system-prompt line telling the assistant to try the docs tool first and fall back to the tracker tool after.
options.explanation: A blanket ordering rule misroutes the opposite case (bug questions) and leaves the vague descriptions, the real selection signal, unfixed.

options.text: Merge both tools into one search tool that queries the two servers and concatenates whatever results come back.
options.explanation: Merging hides the distinction instead of describing it, and mixes stale bug threads with docs in every answer.

options.text: Set tool_choice to force the docs tool on each turn so configuration questions are sure to reach the docs.
options.explanation: Forcing one tool every turn blocks legitimate issue-tracker queries entirely; it replaces selection rather than fixing it.

explanation: Correct: A. Tool descriptions are the main signal the model uses to choose tools; near-identical minimal descriptions cause misrouting. Spelling out inputs, examples, boundaries and when to use each tool fixes selection. Why not the others: B adds a rigid ordering that breaks other queries; C erases the distinction; D forces one tool and disables the other.

prompt: A monorepo holds SQL migration files under `migrations/` folders in 30 different services. The team has eight conventions for them (idempotent statements, guarded DROPs, naming). Putting the conventions in the root CLAUDE.md spends context in every session, including frontend work. How should they be configured?

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md inside each of the 30 migrations folders, generated by a script that keeps the copies in sync.
options.explanation: Thirty duplicated files drift and need tooling to maintain. A single path-scoped rule covers files spread across the tree.

options.text: Put the conventions in a skill with context: fork so they run in a separate context when migrations change.
options.explanation: Skills are invoked on demand, not triggered by the file being edited, and a forked context would keep the conventions away from the editing session.

options.text: Add .claude/rules/migrations.md with paths frontmatter "**/migrations/*.sql" so it loads just for those files.
Keep them in the root CLAUDE.md but move them to the end so they draw less attention during other work.
options.explanation: Position does not stop the text from loading; it still costs context in every session, frontend work included.

explanation: Correct: C. Rules in .claude/rules/ with a paths glob load only when Claude works on matching files, which suits conventions for a file type scattered across many directories. Why not the others: A duplicates thirty files; B relies on manual invocation and isolates the conventions from the edit; D still loads them everywhere.

prompt: A nightly CI job launches Claude Code to find TODO comments older than a year and push them to a team dashboard. The job hangs until its 10-minute timeout, and on the runs that finish, the dashboard importer chokes on the conversational text it receives. Which TWO changes fix the job? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run Claude Code with -p so it works non-interactively and exits instead of waiting for input.
Add "reply in JSON" to the prompt and pull the first brace-delimited block out of stdout with a regex.
options.explanation: Prompt-only JSON with regex extraction is brittle; the CLI can emit machine-parseable output validated against a schema.

options.text: Reuse the engineer's interactive session through --resume so the job inherits their context.
options.explanation: Resuming a personal interactive session does not stop the run from waiting for input and ties CI to one person's history.

options.text: Raise the job timeout from 10 to 60 minutes so the session has time to get past its prompt.
options.explanation: The job is blocked waiting for interactive input; more time only makes it hang longer.

options.text: Add --output-format json with a --json-schema for the findings so the importer can parse them.

explanation: Correct: A and E. -p (--print) runs Claude Code non-interactively so CI jobs do not hang on input, and --output-format json with --json-schema yields machine-parseable findings. Why not the others: B relies on prompt wording and regex parsing; C ties CI to an interactive personal session; D extends a hang rather than removing it.

prompt: The coordinator spends ten turns learning that the `inventory` service uses SQLAlchemy 1.4 with a `BaseRepo` class in `db/base.py`. It then spawns a boilerplate subagent via the Task tool with the prompt "Generate CRUD handlers for the Supplier model, consistent with what we found." The handlers come back written for the Django ORM. What is the fix?

options.text: Add "Task" to the boilerplate subagent's allowedTools so it can consult the coordinator's earlier findings.
options.explanation: "Task" belongs in the coordinator's allowedTools so it can spawn subagents. It does not give a subagent access to anyone's history.

options.text: Spawn the subagent in the same turn as the exploration so it shares the coordinator's working memory.
options.explanation: Timing does not matter: subagents never inherit the coordinator's context, whichever turn they are spawned in.

options.text: Give the subagent a step-by-step procedure naming each file to open, since goal-style prompts confuse it.
options.explanation: Coordinator prompts should state goals and quality criteria, not procedures, and a file list still omits the ORM and base-class findings.

options.text: Subagents don't inherit the coordinator's history; pass the ORM, version and BaseRepo path in the prompt.

explanation: Correct: D. Subagents start with isolated context and receive only what the coordinator passes in their prompt, so prior findings must be stated explicitly. Why not the others: A confuses the coordinator's need for "Task" with context sharing; B assumes shared memory that does not exist; C swaps goals for procedures and still omits the findings.

prompt: The documentation server's `fetch_page` tool answers every failure with `{"isError": true, "content": "Operation failed"}`, whether the server timed out, the slug was malformed or the page is restricted to the security team. Logs show the assistant retrying restricted pages five times in a row. What should the server return instead?

options.text: Keep the message but have the assistant retry each failed call three times with backoff before giving up.
options.explanation: Blind retries waste calls on permission and validation errors that will never succeed; the agent needs to know which kind of failure occurred.

options.text: An errorCategory (transient, validation, permission), an isRetryable flag and a readable description.
An empty content array with no error, so the assistant moves on rather than looping on the same page.
options.explanation: Reporting a failure as an empty success misleads the agent into thinking the page has no content, hiding the access problem.

options.text: The full stack trace in server logs while keeping the client message short to avoid leaking internals.
options.explanation: Server-side logging helps operators but leaves the agent with the same generic message and no way to choose a recovery.

explanation: Correct: B. Structured MCP errors with isError plus a category, a retryable flag and a description let the agent retry transient failures, fix bad input and stop on permission errors. Why not the others: A retries blindly; C disguises a failure as an empty result; D improves logs but not the agent's ability to recover.

prompt: Marco wrote a `/scaffold-endpoint` command that generates a handler, route, schema and test stub in the house style. It lives in his ~/.claude/commands/ folder. The rest of the team wants it, and the tech lead wants changes to it to go through code review like any other file. Where should it live?

options.text: In .claude/commands/ in the repository, so it is version-controlled and available to anyone who clones it.
In each engineer's ~/.claude/commands/, copied there by an onboarding script that pulls the latest version.
options.explanation: Copies in personal folders drift between machines and bypass code review; the project commands folder is the shared location.

options.text: In the project CLAUDE.md, pasted in full so its instructions are loaded at the start of every session.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded context for universal standards. A scaffolding workflow belongs in an on-demand command.

options.text: In ~/.claude.json as an MCP server prompt, so teammates discover it automatically when they connect.
options.explanation: ~/.claude.json is user scope, personal to one machine, so it neither shares the command nor puts it under code review.

explanation: Correct: A. Project commands in .claude/commands/ are committed with the repo, shared with everyone and reviewed like code; ~/.claude/commands/ is personal. Why not the others: B scatters unreviewed copies; C turns an on-demand workflow into always-loaded context; D uses a personal config file.

prompt: An engineer has two requests for Claude Code this week. First, replace the in-house `oldlog` library with structlog across roughly 60 files in five services, deciding how context propagation should work. Second, fix a KeyError in `config/loader.py`, for which they have the full stack trace. How should each be handled?

options.text: Plan mode for both, since any change to a legacy service carries enough risk to need an approved plan first.
options.explanation: A scoped single-file fix with a stack trace is a clear change; forcing a planning phase on it adds overhead without benefit.

options.text: Plan mode for the logging migration and direct execution for the KeyError, which has a known location.
Direct execution for the migration in batches of files, and plan mode for the KeyError since its cause is unclear.
options.explanation: This inverts the guidance: the multi-file migration with design choices needs planning, and the stack trace already pins down the bug.

options.text: Direct execution for both, relying on the test suite to catch any mistakes in either change afterwards.
options.explanation: Jumping straight into a 60-file migration with open design questions risks costly rework that tests catch only after the fact.

explanation: Correct: B. Plan mode fits large, multi-file work with architectural choices, such as a library migration across services; direct execution fits clear, scoped changes like a single-file bug with a stack trace. Why not the others: A over-plans a trivial fix; C inverts the two; D skips planning on the migration.

prompt: The boilerplate generator must call `read_service_manifest` before writing anything, because the manifest names the framework and port conventions. With tool_choice set to "auto", about one run in eight skips it and writes Flask code for services that use FastAPI. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Set tool_choice to "any" for the whole run so the model has to call some tool before replying with text.
options.explanation: "any" guarantees a tool call but not which one; the model could still pick a different tool first and skip the manifest.

options.text: Keep "auto" and add a system-prompt sentence stating that the manifest must be read before writing code.
options.explanation: Prompt guidance is probabilistic and the model already ignores the ordering one run in eight; tool_choice can guarantee it.

options.text: Force {"type": "tool", "name": "read_service_manifest"} on the first request; generate in later turns.
Remove the other tools from the agent so read_service_manifest is the one tool left for it to call at all.
options.explanation: Stripping the toolset breaks the later steps that need file writes and searches; forcing the first call suffices.

explanation: Correct: C. A forced tool_choice of {"type": "tool", "name": ...} guarantees that specific tool runs first; later steps then proceed in follow-up turns. Why not the others: A guarantees some tool, not this one; B stays probabilistic; D removes tools the rest of the workflow needs.

prompt: An engineer new to the legacy quoting service asks Claude Code to "add a cache in front of the pricing lookup." They don't know how often prices change, who updates them, or what should happen if the cache store goes down, and they worry about shipping something subtly wrong. What is the best way to start?

options.text: Have Claude implement a standard LRU cache at once, then review the diff together to see what was missed.
options.explanation: Building first bakes in guesses about invalidation and failure behaviour; the open questions surface only after the work is done.

options.text: Have Claude interview the engineer first about invalidation triggers, staleness and failure handling.
Write one long prompt listing caching best practices so Claude applies the whole list in a single pass.
options.explanation: Generic best practices do not answer service-specific questions such as how often prices change or what a stale price costs.

options.text: Ask Claude to search the web for caching libraries and adopt the most popular one for the quoting service.
options.explanation: Picking a library skips the design questions the engineer cannot yet answer; popularity says nothing about invalidation needs.

explanation: Correct: B. The interview pattern has Claude ask questions that surface considerations the engineer may not have thought of, such as cache invalidation and failure modes, before implementation. Why not the others: A builds on guesses; C applies generic advice to specific unknowns; D chooses tooling before the design is understood.

prompt: A monorepo with `api/`, `web/` and `infra/` packages has a root CLAUDE.md that has grown to 1,400 lines mixing testing rules, API conventions, Terraform style and React guidance. Edits to it cause merge conflicts and nobody can find anything. Which TWO changes improve how these instructions are organised? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Split the topics into separate files under .claude/rules/, such as testing.md and api-conventions.md.
Move the standards into each engineer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so the shared file stays short and tidy.
options.explanation: User-level files are not shared through version control, so teammates would drift apart and new hires would get none of it.

options.text: In each package's CLAUDE.md, @import just the standards files that package needs, e.g. the Terraform guide.
Turn the whole file into one skill so the standards load only when someone invokes the skill by name.
options.explanation: Skills are for on-demand workflows. Universal standards must be present without anyone remembering to invoke them.

options.text: Keep one file but sort its sections by package so Claude can skip the parts that do not apply to a task.
options.explanation: Reordering does not reduce what is loaded or the merge conflicts; one monolith still holds every topic.

explanation: Correct: A and C. Topic files in .claude/rules/ replace a monolithic CLAUDE.md, and @import lets each package pull in only the standards it needs. Why not the others: B moves team standards out of version control; D makes always-needed standards on-demand; E reshuffles the monolith without splitting it.

prompt: The platform team wants every engineer's Claude Code to connect to the company issue tracker through a maintained community MCP server. The server needs an API token, and each engineer has their own. Which TWO steps are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Define the server in the project's .mcp.json and commit it so every engineer gets the same setup.
Write the token value straight into .mcp.json, since the repository is private to employees anyway.
options.explanation: Committing secrets to version control leaks them to anyone with repo access and its history; reference an environment variable instead.

options.text: Reference the token as ${TRACKER_TOKEN} in .mcp.json so each engineer supplies it from their environment.
Add the server to each engineer's ~/.claude.json, the scope meant for shared team configuration.
options.explanation: ~/.claude.json is user scope for personal or experimental servers; shared team servers belong in the project's .mcp.json.

options.text: Build a custom MCP server for the tracker so the team controls it, despite the community server.
options.explanation: Prefer an existing community server for a standard integration; custom servers are for team-specific workflows.

explanation: Correct: A and C. Project-scoped .mcp.json is committed and shared, and environment variable expansion such as ${TRACKER_TOKEN} keeps secrets out of the repository. Why not the others: B commits a secret; D uses the personal user scope for team config; E rebuilds what a maintained community server already provides.

prompt: `search_docs` and `search_issues` both have detailed descriptions with examples, yet whenever an engineer mentions an error, the assistant calls `search_issues`, even for "what does error code E42 mean in the API reference?" The system prompt includes: "When the user mentions an error, look for related issues first." What should the team change?

options.text: Lengthen the search_docs description again, adding more example queries that mention error codes.
options.explanation: The descriptions are already good; the system-prompt keyword rule outranks them, so more examples will not change the routing.

options.text: Lower the sampling temperature so the assistant follows the tool descriptions more consistently.
options.explanation: The assistant is consistently following an instruction, not behaving randomly; temperature does not remove the conflicting rule.

options.text: Merge both tools into one search tool so the assistant never has to choose between them on errors.
options.explanation: Merging removes a useful distinction and mixes doc pages with bug threads; the cause is the prompt wording, not the tool split.

options.text: Reword the system-prompt line, whose keyword trigger overrides the descriptions, to say when each applies.

explanation: Correct: D. Keyword-sensitive system-prompt instructions can override good tool descriptions, so the prompt must be reviewed and reworded. Why not the others: A improves descriptions that are not the problem; B treats deterministic instruction-following as randomness; C removes a meaningful tool boundary instead of fixing the prompt.

prompt: Traces show that at the start of nearly every task the assistant makes 15 to 20 `list_pages` and `search_docs` calls on the documentation server just to discover which sections and runbooks exist, before doing any real work. How should the docs MCP server change?

options.text: Raise the per-task tool-call limit so the discovery calls no longer crowd out the useful work afterwards.
options.explanation: This accepts the waste rather than removing it; the agent still spends 15 to 20 calls and their context learning what exists.

options.text: Add a tool that returns the full text of each docs page in one call, replacing the separate searches.
options.explanation: Dumping every page's text floods the context with content the task mostly does not need; a catalog is what is missing.

options.text: Hard-code the 40 most-used doc URLs into the system prompt and remove the search tool from the server.
options.explanation: A static list goes stale and covers few pages, and removing search blocks lookups for anything off the list.

options.text: Expose the documentation hierarchy as an MCP resource so the agent sees the catalog without tool calls.

explanation: Correct: D. MCP resources expose content catalogs such as documentation hierarchies, giving the agent visibility into what exists without exploratory tool calls. Why not the others: A tolerates the waste; B floods context with full text; C hard-codes a stale subset and removes search.

prompt: The assistant's "code explainer" subagent receives all 22 tools available to the system: built-ins plus tools from four MCP servers. Engineers report that while answering "how does this module work?" it occasionally files tickets with `create_issue` or edits files. What is the best fix?

options.text: Give the explainer only the read-oriented tools its role needs, such as Read, Grep, Glob and search_docs.
Add a prompt sentence asking the explainer not to create issues or edit files unless someone requests it.
options.explanation: Prompt guidance stays probabilistic and leaves 22 tools to choose from; removing out-of-role tools prevents the misuse outright.

options.text: Keep all 22 tools but order them so the read-only ones appear first in the list the subagent receives.
options.explanation: Ordering does not stop the subagent from picking out-of-role tools, and the oversized toolset still degrades selection.

options.text: Move create_issue to a separate MCP server so it is discovered after the read tools when connecting.
options.explanation: Tools from all configured servers are available together after discovery; moving a tool does not hide it.

explanation: Correct: A. Scoping tools to each role avoids the selection degradation of large toolsets and stops out-of-role tools from being misused. Why not the others: B relies on probabilistic prompting; C keeps every tool available; D misunderstands MCP discovery, which makes all servers' tools available together.

prompt: The assistant needs to change the fallback in one function of `legacy_parser.py`, but its Edit call fails: the anchor text `return None` appears seven times in the file. What should it do next?

options.text: Use Bash with sed to replace the `return None` occurrences in the file in a single command.
options.explanation: sed would rewrite all seven occurrences, changing six functions that were not meant to change.

options.text: Retry the same Edit call, since a repeat attempt resolves the anchor against the nearest function.
options.explanation: Edit requires a unique text match; retrying the same non-unique anchor fails the same way.

options.text: Grep for the line number, then pass that number to Edit in place of the anchor text it expects.
options.explanation: Edit works by matching unique text, not line numbers, so the call would not do what is intended.

options.text: Read the file to locate the right occurrence, then Write the corrected file back in full.

explanation: Correct: D. Edit makes targeted changes by unique text match; when the anchor is not unique, reading the file and writing it back with the change is the fallback. Why not the others: A changes every occurrence; B repeats a call that cannot succeed; C passes Edit a line number it does not accept.

prompt: One automated chore resets test fixtures by calling `drop_test_database`. The system prompt says to call `confirm_environment` first and proceed only if it reports a non-production target. Across roughly 400 runs the agent complied every time but one, when it dropped a database on a production connection string. What should the team do?

options.text: Move the instruction to the top of the system prompt and repeat it in capitals next to the tool list.
options.explanation: Stronger wording still leaves a probabilistic control; for a destructive operation the check must be enforced in code.

options.text: Add a gate in code that blocks drop_test_database until confirm_environment returns non-production.
Add few-shot examples showing the agent calling confirm_environment before each drop_test_database.
options.explanation: Examples improve consistency but do not guarantee it; prompts alone keep a non-zero failure rate.

options.text: Have the agent state its confidence that the target is safe and proceed only when it reports over 90%.
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and is not a deterministic check of the environment.

explanation: Correct: B. When compliance must be deterministic, programmatic prerequisite gates enforce the order; prompt guidance has a non-zero failure rate, as the one bad run shows. Why not the others: A and C strengthen prompting, which stays probabilistic; D relies on uncalibrated self-reported confidence.

prompt: The tracker's `find_related_issues` tool returns `{"results": []}` both when nothing matches and when its service token has expired. Last week the token lapsed and the assistant told several engineers "there are no known bugs in this module" about a module with eleven open crash reports. What should change?

options.text: Have the assistant warn engineers that any empty result might be an error and to check the tracker by hand.
options.explanation: This pushes the problem to users and casts doubt on genuine empty results; the tool itself must distinguish the two cases.

options.text: On auth failure return isError with a permission category, so an empty list only ever means no matches.
Have the tool retry automatically on empty results, since a second call often surfaces hidden matches.
options.explanation: An expired token fails on every retry, and real no-match results get pointless extra calls; the failure stays hidden.

options.text: Return a generic "Operation failed" error for empty results so empty data is not presented as fact.
options.explanation: This turns genuine no-match answers into errors and gives no information on what failed, blocking recovery.

explanation: Correct: B. An access failure is not a valid empty result: the tool should flag it with isError and a category so the agent can report the outage, leaving empty results to mean no matches. Why not the others: A shifts the burden to users; C retries a failure that cannot succeed; D replaces one confusion with a generic error.

prompt: The company runs a code-search MCP server whose `code_search` tool indexes all 200 repositories and resolves cross-repo references; its description reads "Search code." Asked who calls `PaymentClient.charge`, the assistant uses built-in Grep in the local checkout and misses callers in four other repos. What is the best fix?

options.text: Remove Grep from the assistant's built-in tools so code_search becomes the single search option left.
options.explanation: Grep remains the right tool for quick searches in the local checkout; removing it hurts those tasks instead of fixing selection.

options.text: Expand code_search's description: it covers all 200 repos, resolves cross-repo refs, and when to prefer it.
Clone all 200 repositories into the workspace so that Grep can reach callers that live in other repos.
options.explanation: This is heavy and slow, and Grep still cannot resolve cross-repo references the way the indexed server does.

options.text: Move the code-search server from project to user scope so its tools get priority over the built-in ones.
options.explanation: Scope controls who has the server configured, not selection priority; the vague description is still the problem.

explanation: Correct: B. When an MCP tool's description is minimal, the agent prefers familiar built-ins like Grep; enriching the description with its capabilities and when to use it fixes selection. Why not the others: A removes a tool that is right for local searches; C brute-forces around the issue without cross-repo resolution; D confuses configuration scope with priority.

prompt: The assistant builds incident timelines from three MCP servers: the issue tracker returns Unix epoch seconds, the docs server returns ISO 8601 strings and the CI server returns integers like `20261029143000`. Timelines frequently put a deploy after the incident it caused. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Describe the three formats in the system prompt and ask the model to convert them before comparing dates.
options.explanation: Prompted conversion is probabilistic and easy to slip on long timelines; a hook normalises the data deterministically.

options.text: Ask each server's owners to change their API output and hold the timeline feature until they have done so.
options.explanation: This blocks the feature on other teams and may never happen; the agent can normalise results on its own side.

options.text: Add a PostToolUse hook that converts each tool's timestamps to ISO 8601 before the model sees the results.
Add a pre-call hook that blocks calls to any server whose timestamps are not already ISO 8601 formatted.
options.explanation: Pre-call hooks intercept requests for policy reasons; blocking two of three servers removes the data the timeline needs.

explanation: Correct: C. PostToolUse hooks transform tool results before the model sees them, such as normalising mixed timestamp formats, which is a deterministic fix. Why not the others: A relies on probabilistic in-prompt conversion; B depends on other teams; D blocks needed calls instead of transforming results.

prompt: After a long session in which the assistant mapped the legacy `orders` module, an engineer wants to compare two refactoring routes: a strangler wrapper around it, or an in-place rewrite. Both should start from the same understanding, and work on one route must not bleed into the other. How should they proceed?

options.text: Use fork_session to branch two sessions from the shared mapping and explore one route in each branch.
Stay in the same session: explore the wrapper first, then ask the model to set it aside for the rewrite.
options.explanation: Everything said about the wrapper stays in the context and colours the rewrite analysis; asking the model to forget does not remove it.

options.text: Open two fresh sessions and have each one redo the full module mapping before exploring its route.
options.explanation: This throws away the existing baseline and may produce two different mappings, so the comparison no longer starts from shared ground.

options.text: Run --resume on the same session in two terminals so that both routes add to one shared history.
options.explanation: Resuming one session twice does not create independent branches; both routes would land in the same history and mix.

explanation: Correct: A. fork_session branches from a shared baseline so two approaches can be explored independently from the same starting context. Why not the others: B lets one route contaminate the other; C discards the shared baseline; D mixes both routes into one history instead of branching.

prompt: The tracker's `get_issue` returns about 70 fields per call: watchers, custom fields, the full changelog. Twenty-five lookups into investigating a recurring outage, the assistant's context is mostly issue JSON, and it has lost the root-cause facts it established early (affected version 4.2.1, first seen 3 March). What should the team change?

options.text: Summarise the conversation every ten turns and let each summary replace the earlier issue details in full.
options.explanation: Progressive summarisation tends to drop exact versions, dates and numbers, which are the facts already being lost.

options.text: Trim each get_issue result to the few fields the task uses and keep key findings in a persistent facts block.
Switch to a model with a larger context window so all 70 fields from each lookup can stay in the history.
options.explanation: A bigger window postpones the bloat but keeps the noise, and facts buried in the middle of long contexts are still missed.

options.text: Drop the conversation history between turns and resend just the newest message to keep requests small.
options.explanation: The model needs the full history each request; dropping it discards the investigation's findings entirely.

explanation: Correct: B. Trimming verbose tool output to relevant fields stops it crowding the context, and a persistent facts block keeps versions and dates outside any summarised history. Why not the others: A relies on summarisation that loses exact facts; C keeps the noise and the lost-in-the-middle risk; D throws away the history the model needs.

prompt: An engineer asks: "List the React test files under packages/, and show me every file that imports the `useLegacyAuth` hook." Which TWO tool calls fit these requests? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Grep with the pattern **/*.test.tsx to list the test files by their paths
options.explanation: Grep searches file contents, not paths; a path glob belongs in Glob.

options.text: Glob with the pattern useLegacyAuth to find files importing the hook
options.explanation: Glob matches file paths, so it cannot see which files import a symbol; that is a content search.

options.text: Glob with packages/**/*.test.tsx to list the test files by their paths
Grep for useLegacyAuth to find files whose contents import the hook
Read each file under packages/, then filter imports and tests from it
options.explanation: Reading everything up front wastes context; Glob and Grep answer both questions directly.

explanation: Correct: C and D. Glob matches file paths, so it finds test files by pattern; Grep searches file contents, so it finds imports of a hook. Why not the others: A uses Grep for a path pattern; B uses Glob for a content search; E reads everything up front instead of searching.

prompt: An engineer wants every usage of the legacy `billing_client` module before deprecating it. Grep for `billing_client` finds only three hits, but most code imports from `core/clients/__init__.py`, which re-exports the module's functions as `charge`, `refund_payment` and `BillingSession`. What should the assistant do?

options.text: Report that billing_client is barely used, since Grep already scanned each file's contents for the name.
options.explanation: Grep only found direct references; code that imports the re-exported names never mentions billing_client.

options.text: Use Glob with **/billing_client* to find the files named after the module and treat those as usages.
options.explanation: Glob matches file names, which shows where the module lives, not who calls it through the wrapper.

options.text: Read the wrapper to list each name it exports, then Grep for each exported name across the codebase.
Read every Python file in the repository up front so no indirect usage of the module can be missed.
options.explanation: Reading everything floods context; following the wrapper's exports with targeted Grep finds indirect usages efficiently.

explanation: Correct: C. To trace usage through wrapper modules, find all the names the wrapper exports and search for each one. Why not the others: A trusts a search that cannot see re-exported names; B matches file paths rather than usages; D reads the whole codebase instead of building understanding incrementally.

prompt: The review prompt contains the line "Check that code comments are accurate." On a recent pull request touching a date-parsing module, the bot left 23 comment-related notes, almost all suggesting nicer wording for docstrings that were correct. Developers now resolve these notes without reading them. How should that instruction be rewritten?

options.text: Flag a comment only when the behaviour it describes contradicts what the code actually does.
Be conservative and report only the comments you are highly confident are genuinely inaccurate.
options.explanation: Vague caution words such as "be conservative" or "high confidence" do not improve precision; the model still has no definition of what makes a comment inaccurate.

options.text: Keep the instruction as written but cap comment findings at three per pull request.
options.explanation: A cap trims volume arbitrarily and can drop a real contradiction while keeping wording nits, because the criterion itself is still undefined.

options.text: Have the reviewer score its confidence for each comment finding and post those over 0.8.
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and filtering on it leaves the underlying criterion (what counts as inaccurate) as vague as before.

explanation: Correct: A. Explicit, categorical criteria beat vague ones: defining an inaccurate comment as one whose claimed behaviour contradicts the code removes the wording suggestions entirely. Why not the others: B relies on caution words that do not raise precision; C caps volume without defining the target; D filters on uncalibrated self-reported confidence instead of fixing the criterion.

prompt: On its first push, PR #4127 received six review comments. The author then pushed two commits that address four of them. The rerun posted eight comments: the two still-open issues reworded, the four already-fixed ones again, and two new ones. The author complains the bot ignores their fixes. What should change in the rerun?

options.text: Delete every earlier bot comment before each run so the thread shows only the latest full review.
options.explanation: Deleting history hides the duplication but the run still re-reports fixed issues, and reviewers lose the record of what was raised and resolved.

options.text: Review only the files touched by the newest commits and skip the rest of the diff on reruns.
options.explanation: Unaddressed findings in untouched files and cross-file effects of the new commits would be missed; the run still lacks the earlier findings to compare against.

options.text: Resume the first review's session with --resume so the model recalls what it posted earlier.
options.explanation: The resumed session carries tool results from the old code, and nothing tells it to limit output to new or unaddressed issues; passing prior findings explicitly is the documented approach.

options.text: Pass the prior findings into the rerun and ask only for new issues or ones still unaddressed.

explanation: Correct: D. On re-review after new commits, include the earlier findings in the context and ask the model to report only new or still-unaddressed issues, so fixed items are not reposted. Why not the others: A hides the history without changing what is reported; B misses issues outside the latest commits; C reuses stale context and gives no instruction to filter.

prompt: A new pipeline step runs `claude "Review this diff for bugs"`. The step sits idle until the runner kills it at the 60-minute timeout. The team also wants the following step to post each finding as an inline comment on the right file and line, but the output it has seen so far in local tests is free-form prose. Which two changes address these problems? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run Claude Code with -p so it handles the prompt non-interactively, prints the result and exits.
Pipe the yes command into the process so any interactive confirmation is answered automatically.
options.explanation: This is a fragile workaround for a session that was started interactively; -p is the documented non-interactive mode and avoids waiting for input at all.

options.text: Add --output-format json with --json-schema describing file, line, severity and message fields.
Tell the model in the prompt to write each finding as "file:line - message" and parse with a regex.
options.explanation: Prompt-only formatting is not guaranteed; any stray prose breaks the regex. A JSON schema gives machine-parseable output the posting step can rely on.

options.text: Raise the job timeout to 120 minutes so the review has time to finish before the runner stops it.
options.explanation: The job is not slow, it is waiting for interactive input; a longer timeout only wastes more runner time before the same failure.

explanation: Correct: A and C. The -p (--print) flag runs Claude Code non-interactively so CI does not hang waiting for input, and --output-format json with --json-schema yields structured findings that can be posted as inline PR comments. Why not the others: B is a brittle hack around interactive mode; D depends on the model following a prose format; E treats a hang as slowness.

prompt: To cut noise, the team appended "Only report high-confidence issues. Be conservative." to the review prompt. Over the next 200 pull requests the share of dismissed comments moved from 38% to 36%, and two real injection bugs that the old prompt caught went unreported. What should the team do next?

options.text: Strengthen the wording to "Report an issue only if you are at least 95% sure it is a real defect."
options.explanation: A numeric certainty threshold is the same vague confidence instruction in stronger words; the model's self-assessed certainty does not track precision.

options.text: Replace it with categories to report (logic bugs, security flaws) and to skip (style, local idioms).
Add a second step asking the same session to re-read its findings and delete any it now doubts.
options.explanation: A model is unlikely to question its own reasoning in the same session, and the step still has no criteria for what should be reported.

options.text: Turn on extended thinking for the review so the model reasons for longer before it flags anything.
options.explanation: More reasoning does not tell the model which categories matter; without explicit criteria the noisy categories remain.

explanation: Correct: B. Instructions like "be conservative" or "only high-confidence" do not improve precision; categorical criteria that say what to report and what to skip do, without suppressing real security findings. Why not the others: A is the same vague instruction with a number attached; C is self-review in the same session without criteria; D adds reasoning but no definition of what to flag.

prompt: The pipeline's test-generation step proposed 14 tests for `invoice_totals.py`. A reviewer noticed that 11 of them assert exactly what `tests/test_invoice_totals.py` already checks, only with different function names. What change makes the step propose useful tests?

options.text: Add "do not write tests that already exist in the repository" to the prompt and leave the rest as is.
options.explanation: The model cannot avoid duplicating tests it has never seen; the instruction is unenforceable without the existing test file in context.

options.text: Include the existing test file for the module in the context and ask for cases it does not yet cover.
Post-process the output with a script that drops any test whose function name already exists.
options.explanation: The duplicates here have different names but the same assertions, so a name check would let nearly all of them through.

options.text: Generate tests only for modules that have no test file at all and skip any module already covered.
options.explanation: Partly tested modules often have the most valuable gaps; skipping them avoids duplicates by giving up on coverage where it matters.

explanation: Correct: B. Giving the test-generation run the existing test files lets it see what is covered and propose only missing cases. Why not the others: A asks the model to avoid tests it cannot see; C matches on names while the duplicates differ in name; D throws away gap-filling for partly tested modules.

prompt: When Priya runs the review command on her laptop, it reliably flags raw SQL written outside the repository layer. The CI run on the same branch never does. Investigation shows the rule exists only in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` on Priya's machine. What is the right fix?

options.text: Move the rule into the project CLAUDE.md committed to the repository, so CI and teammates load it.
Copy Priya's whole ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md into the CI runner's home directory as part of the job setup step.
options.explanation: That ships her personal preferences to CI, keeps the team rule out of version control and lets the two copies drift apart.

options.text: Add the rule to the pull request template so the reviewer reads it along with each change.
options.explanation: Authors can edit or delete template text, so the rule becomes optional per PR instead of a standard every run loads.

options.text: Ask Priya to trigger the review from her own machine so her personal configuration applies.
options.explanation: This ties the pipeline to one person's laptop and still leaves every other developer and the CI runner without the rule.

explanation: Correct: A. User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is personal and not shared through version control; team standards belong in the project CLAUDE.md so CI runs and all teammates pick them up. Why not the others: B copies personal settings and creates drift; C makes the rule depend on PR text authors control; D makes CI depend on one developer's machine.

prompt: A refactoring PR touches 38 files. In a single review pass the bot left detailed notes on the first nine files, one-line generic remarks on the rest, and missed that `api/client.ts` now sends a field `server/handler.ts` no longer accepts. How should the review be structured for changes of this size?

options.text: Raise the output token limit so the single review pass has room to discuss every file in full depth.
options.explanation: The problem is attention spread across 38 files in one pass, not output space; a longer answer from the same pass stays shallow on later files.

options.text: Split the files into four random groups and review each group in its own parallel pass.
options.explanation: Random grouping can separate the client and handler, and with no integration pass nothing checks interfaces across groups.

options.text: Review each file in a focused pass, then run a separate integration pass across file interfaces.
Process the files in reverse order on alternate runs so detailed coverage evens out over time.
options.explanation: This shifts which files get shallow treatment instead of removing it, and still never checks how the files interact.

explanation: Correct: C. Per-file passes keep attention focused on each file, and a dedicated cross-file integration pass catches interface mismatches like the client-handler field. Why not the others: A adds output room without fixing attention dilution; B loses cross-group interactions; D rotates the blind spot instead of removing it.

prompt: Twelve services each keep schema migrations under `services/<name>/db/migrations/`. The review rules for migrations (no column drop without a backfill, no lock-heavy index builds) currently sit in the root CLAUDE.md, so they load for every run, including frontend-only PRs. Where should these rules live?

options.text: In a CLAUDE.md file with the migration rules placed inside each one of the twelve migrations folders.
options.explanation: Twelve copies of the same rules drift apart as they are edited; path-scoped rules suit file types spread across the tree.

options.text: In a skill that developers are told to invoke whenever their pull request touches a migration.
options.explanation: Skills load on demand, so the rules depend on someone remembering to invoke one; they would not apply automatically to migration edits.

options.text: In a .claude/rules/ file whose paths frontmatter globs services/*/db/migrations/** for those files.
In the root CLAUDE.md still, under a heading saying the section applies to migrations only.
options.explanation: A heading does not stop the text from loading; the rules still consume context on every run, including frontend PRs.

explanation: Correct: C. A .claude/rules/ file with a paths glob loads only when matching files are involved, which suits a file type scattered across many directories and saves context elsewhere. Why not the others: A duplicates the rules twelve times; B relies on manual invocation; D still loads the text everywhere.

prompt: A month of dismissal data by finding category: security 4% dismissed, null-safety 6%, naming 61%. Engineering managers report that developers have started skimming past all bot comments, and a valid SQL injection warning sat unread for two days. What is the best immediate step?

options.text: Keep every category enabled but add a note to naming comments marking them as low priority.
options.explanation: The noisy comments still appear on every PR, so they keep eroding trust in the accurate categories that sit beside them.

options.text: Lower naming findings to an "info" severity so they are shown collapsed in the review thread.
options.explanation: Collapsed noise is still noise; developers learn the bot is often wrong, and the naming criteria are never fixed.

options.text: Ask developers to thumbs-down wrong comments so the model gradually learns what to stop flagging.
options.explanation: Reactions on PR comments do not change the model or the prompt; nothing in the pipeline learns from them.

options.text: Disable the naming category for now while its criteria are rewritten and tested on past PRs.

explanation: Correct: D. A high false-positive category erodes trust in accurate ones, so temporarily turning it off while its prompt is fixed restores confidence in security and null-safety findings. Why not the others: A and B keep the noise visible; C assumes a feedback loop that does not exist.

prompt: The team's `.claude/skills/deps-audit/SKILL.md` audits dependency changes. When developers invoke it locally it dumps about 3,000 lines of lockfile analysis into their session, and last week it ran `npm install` and modified `package-lock.json` mid-audit. Which two frontmatter settings fix this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: argument-hint asking for a package name, so each run audits a single dependency.
options.explanation: argument-hint only prompts for a parameter; output can still flood the session and nothing stops install commands from running.

options.text: context: fork, so the audit runs in an isolated sub-agent and returns only a summary.
allowed-tools limited to read-only tools, so the skill cannot run install commands.
A move to ~/.claude/skills/, so the output stays in each developer's own session.
options.explanation: Location changes who can see the skill, not how it runs; the output would still fill the session and install commands still run.

options.text: A conversion into a CLAUDE.md section, so it loads at startup and needs no invocation.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded standards; putting a workflow there costs context on every session and does not contain its output or tools.

explanation: Correct: B and C. context: fork runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so verbose output does not pollute the main session, and allowed-tools restricts which tools the skill may use while it runs. Why not the others: A only collects a parameter; D changes scope, not behaviour; E turns an on-demand workflow into always-loaded context.
