prompt: The review prompt lists the parts each comment body should contain: location, issue, severity and suggested fix. In practice some comments are a single vague sentence, others run to four paragraphs, and roughly a third omit the suggested fix. What change most directly makes the comments consistent?

options.text: Repeat the list of required parts in capital letters at both the start and end of the prompt.
options.explanation: Repetition and emphasis restate the same instruction the model already reads inconsistently; it still has no picture of a finished comment.

options.text: Lower the maximum output length so the model is pushed into shorter, more uniform comments.
options.explanation: A length cap truncates long comments and can cut off the fix, but does nothing to make short comments include the missing parts.

options.text: Add a rule telling the reviewer to "be consistent" and to "follow exactly the format described above".
options.explanation: A generic consistency instruction adds no information about what a good comment looks like, so behaviour is unlikely to change.

options.text: Add three example comments showing location, issue, severity and fix for different kinds of bug.

explanation: Correct: D. Few-shot examples are the most effective way to get a consistent output format when instructions alone are followed inconsistently; varied examples show the expected structure without overfitting to one bug. Why not the others: A only repeats the instruction; B truncates without adding missing parts; C adds no concrete guidance.

prompt: In a monorepo, `packages/payments` must follow `docs/standards/pci.md` and `packages/web` must follow `docs/standards/a11y.md`. The root CLAUDE.md currently inlines both documents, and the bot leaves PCI comments on CSS-only web PRs. Which setup gives each package's reviews the right standards?

options.text: Paste both standards documents in full into root CLAUDE.md under clearly labelled headings.
options.explanation: Labelled headings still load everywhere, so web reviews keep seeing PCI rules; this is the current problem with more text.

options.text: Keep the root file and tell the reviewer in the CI prompt to ignore standards that look irrelevant.
options.explanation: This asks the model to guess relevance every run, which is exactly where it is failing now; the irrelevant rules still fill context.

options.text: Put both standards in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md on the CI runner so that they load on every run.
options.explanation: User-level files are not version-controlled, are invisible to teammates and would still load both standards for every package.

options.text: Give each package its own CLAUDE.md that uses @import to pull in only its own standards file.

explanation: Correct: D. Directory-level CLAUDE.md files apply to work inside their package, and @import lets each one pull in only the standards file it needs. Why not the others: A and B still load both standards for every PR; C moves team rules into an unshared user-level file and does not scope them.

prompt: Generated unit tests keep building `Order` objects by hand and stubbing HTTP calls with ad hoc mocks. The team's convention is to use the factories in `tests/factories.py` and to keep unit tests free of network access. Reviewers have rewritten about half of the generated tests this sprint. What is the durable fix?

options.text: Add a line about the factories to the PR template so authors remind the generator on each PR.
options.explanation: PR templates are filled in by authors and are not reliably part of the generator's context; the convention would depend on each author.

options.text: Have reviewers keep rejecting non-conforming tests until the generator picks up the pattern.
options.explanation: The model does not learn from rejected PRs between runs; reviewers would keep rewriting tests indefinitely.

options.text: Document the fixtures, factories and testing rules in the project CLAUDE.md that CI runs load.
Reduce the number of generated tests per PR so the model gives each one more careful attention.
options.explanation: Fewer tests do not tell the model about the factories or the no-network rule, so each test would still be written the wrong way.

explanation: Correct: C. CLAUDE.md supplies testing standards, fixtures and conventions to every CI run, so documenting the factories and no-network rule there fixes the cause. Why not the others: A depends on authors and templates; B assumes learning between runs that does not happen; D changes volume, not knowledge.

prompt: The prompt says "flag swallowed exceptions". The bot correctly flags `except Exception: pass` in a worker, but it also flags request handlers written as `except Exception: logger.exception(...); raise`, which re-raise after logging and are the team's standard pattern. How should the prompt be improved?

options.text: Add "do not flag exception handlers" to the skip list so these comments stop appearing on pull requests at all.
options.explanation: That silences the genuine swallowed-exception findings along with the false ones; the category would stop catching real defects.

options.text: Add examples contrasting a log-and-re-raise handler (acceptable, with reasoning) and a silent pass (flag).
Ask for a confidence score on exception findings and post them only above a fixed threshold.
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence does not encode the distinction between re-raising and swallowing, so the false positives may score high.

options.text: List every module that uses the re-raise pattern and exclude those files from review entirely.
options.explanation: Excluding files hides every other kind of bug in them and must be updated as the pattern spreads; it does not teach the distinction.

explanation: Correct: B. Targeted few-shot examples that show an acceptable pattern next to a real issue, with the reasoning for each, teach the model the distinction and generalise to new code. Why not the others: A removes real findings too; C filters on uncalibrated confidence; D blinds review of whole files.

prompt: The review output includes a required `linked_ticket` field validated against `^PAY-\d+$`. Validation fails on 18% of runs and the pipeline retries up to three times with the errors. Retries succeed when the model wrote `pay-123` in lowercase, but never succeed on PRs whose description mentions no ticket at all. What should change?

options.text: Make linked_ticket nullable for PRs with no ticket, and keep retries for format errors such as case.
Raise the retry limit to six attempts and include the full validation error text along with every retry.
options.explanation: Retries cannot recover information that is absent from the source; more attempts only add cost or push the model to invent a ticket.

options.text: Tell the model to infer a ticket ID from the branch name or commit history when none is given.
options.explanation: This invites fabricated ticket IDs that pass the pattern but are wrong, which is worse than an honest missing value.

options.text: Drop the pattern check on linked_ticket so the pipeline accepts whatever value the model returns.
options.explanation: Removing validation loses the format fixes that retries were handling and lets malformed or invented values reach downstream.

explanation: Correct: A. Retries with specific errors fix format problems, but they fail when the information is not in the source; a nullable field lets the model report absence honestly. Why not the others: B retries a case retries cannot fix; C encourages fabrication; D throws away useful validation.

prompt: Marco wrote a `/triage-flaky` slash command in `~/.claude/commands/` that inspects recent CI failures and labels likely flaky tests. Several teammates want the same command, and the platform team would like the pipeline to use it too. What should Marco do?

options.text: Move it to .claude/commands/ in the repository so it is version-controlled and shared with the team.
Ask each teammate to copy his command file by hand into their own personal ~/.claude/commands/ directory.
options.explanation: Hand-copied personal files drift as Marco edits his version, and the CI runner still would not have the command.

options.text: Paste the command's prompt into root CLAUDE.md so it is loaded at the start of every session.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md is always-loaded standards; a task workflow there costs context in every session and is no longer invoked on demand.

options.text: Register the command as an MCP server in .mcp.json so every Claude Code client can discover it.
options.explanation: MCP servers expose tools and resources from external systems; a prompt-based slash command belongs in the commands directory.

explanation: Correct: A. Project commands in .claude/commands/ are committed and shared with everyone who clones the repo, including CI, while ~/.claude/commands/ is personal. Why not the others: B creates unversioned copies; C turns an on-demand workflow into always-loaded context; D uses the wrong mechanism.

prompt: A validator checks that every finding's line number falls inside a changed hunk before it is posted. About 7% of findings fail because they point at unchanged lines several lines away from the real problem. Today a failure triggers a rerun with exactly the same prompt, which fixes fewer than half of them. How should the retry be built?

options.text: Drop any finding that fails validation and post the remainder without running a retry at all.
options.explanation: Most of these findings describe real issues with a wrong location; discarding them loses valid feedback that a targeted retry would recover.

options.text: Resend the same prompt with a higher temperature so the second attempt lands on different lines.
options.explanation: Randomness does not tell the model what was wrong; it may move the line number to another invalid place.

options.text: Retry with the diff, the failed findings and the specific errors naming each out-of-range line.
Retry with only the validator's short "invalid output, try again" message to keep the prompt small.
options.explanation: A generic error gives no clue which findings or lines failed, so the model has nothing concrete to correct.

explanation: Correct: C. Effective retries include the original input, the failed output and the specific validation errors, so the model can correct exactly the misplaced line numbers. Why not the others: A discards real findings; B relies on chance; D gives no actionable error information.

prompt: Developers dismiss roughly 30% of bot comments without changing code. The team wants to fix the prompt but cannot tell which kinds of finding are being dismissed, because comments on a missing await and on an unused import look much the same in the data. What should be added to the pipeline?

options.text: A free-text rationale paragraph on each comment that explains the finding for the developer.
options.explanation: Prose rationales help readers but are hard to aggregate; they do not give a stable label to group dismissals by.

options.text: A self-reported confidence score on each finding, dropping the lowest-scoring third of findings each run.
options.explanation: This filters blindly on uncalibrated scores and still gives no insight into which rule or pattern produces dismissed comments.

options.text: A weekly survey asking developers which bot comments they found least useful in general.
options.explanation: Survey answers are vague and recall-based; they cannot be tied to specific findings and patterns the way per-finding data can.

options.text: A detected_pattern field on each finding, joined with dismissal data to see which rules misfire.

explanation: Correct: D. Recording which pattern triggered each finding lets the team correlate dismissals with specific rules and fix the prompts that produce false positives. Why not the others: A is unstructured; B filters without diagnosing; C cannot be linked to individual findings.

prompt: The CI bot keeps flagging use of the deprecated `legacyAuth` client. The team decides to migrate to the new auth SDK: 52 files across four services, with two candidate approaches (an adapter shim or a direct rewrite of call sites). A developer opens Claude Code locally to start. How should they begin?

options.text: Use direct execution file by file, starting with the service that has the most call sites.
options.explanation: Direct execution suits clear, scoped changes; starting edits before the approach is chosen risks reworking dozens of files.

options.text: Let the CI pipeline produce the migration as suggested changes on the next pull request.
options.explanation: PR review comments are for feedback on a change, not for designing a four-service migration with competing approaches.

options.text: Use plan mode to explore call sites and compare shim versus rewrite, then execute the plan.
Have Claude apply the shim everywhere right away and revert later if the test suite objects.
options.explanation: This commits to one approach without comparing it, across 52 files, and relies on tests to reveal design problems after the fact.

explanation: Correct: C. Plan mode fits large, multi-file work with several viable approaches: explore and decide first, then execute the chosen plan directly. Why not the others: A and D edit before choosing an approach; B uses review comments for design work they are not meant for.

prompt: Two jobs drive most API spend: a pre-merge review that developers wait on before merging, and a nightly job that proposes tests for coverage gaps across 400 modules. Finance proposes moving both to the Message Batches API for the discount. What is the right response?

options.text: Move both, since the 50% saving outweighs an occasional slow batch result on the pre-merge review job.
options.explanation: Batches have up to a 24-hour window and no latency SLA; a blocking merge check cannot tolerate that.

options.text: Move neither, because batch requests cannot include tool definitions or output schemas.
options.explanation: Batch requests can carry the same parameters as normal requests; the limit is no multi-turn tool loop within one request.

options.text: Move only the pre-merge review, because it runs most often and so drives most of the spend.
options.explanation: Frequency does not make it latency-tolerant; developers waiting up to a day on merges is unacceptable.

options.text: Move only the nightly test job; the pre-merge check stays synchronous because it blocks merges.

explanation: Correct: D. The Message Batches API saves about 50% but has no latency guarantee, so it suits latency-tolerant work like nightly test generation, not blocking pre-merge checks. Why not the others: A and C put a blocking check on a 24-hour window; B misstates batch capabilities.

prompt: The bot reported that `parse_duration()` mishandles inputs like "1h30m" and "0s". A developer asked Claude Code to fix it, and after three rounds of "still wrong for some inputs", each fix broke a case that previously worked. What approach should the developer switch to?

options.text: Write tests first covering the edge cases, such as "0s" and "1h30m", then iterate on failing output.
Describe the expected behaviour again in longer, more detailed prose with stronger emphasis on the edge cases.
options.explanation: More prose is what has already been read inconsistently; it gives no objective signal of which inputs pass or regress.

options.text: Ask Claude to rewrite parse_duration from scratch in one pass without reading the old version.
options.explanation: A blind rewrite has no specification of the edge cases either, so it is likely to reintroduce the same or new failures.

options.text: Fix each reported input in a separate fresh session so earlier attempts do not bias the next.
options.explanation: Isolated fixes cannot see each other, which is how regressions crept in; nothing checks earlier cases still pass.

explanation: Correct: A. Test-driven iteration gives an objective target: write tests covering the edge cases, then share the failing output each round so fixes cannot silently break earlier cases. Why not the others: B repeats the ambiguous prose; C rewrites without a specification; D hides regressions between sessions.

prompt: The nightly test-proposal batch had 400 requests. 377 succeeded; 23 failed with errors saying the input exceeded the context window, all for modules containing very large generated files. What should the pipeline do next?

options.text: Resubmit only the 23 failed custom_ids, with those oversized modules split into smaller chunks.
Resubmit the entire 400-request batch unchanged, since failures like these are usually transient.
options.explanation: Context overflow is deterministic for the same input, and resending 377 successful requests doubles cost for no benefit.

options.text: Resubmit the 23 failed requests unchanged in a new batch, hoping the next run has more room.
options.explanation: The inputs are too large for the context window; sending them again unchanged will fail the same way.

options.text: Find the failed requests by their position in the results file and resubmit those positions split up.
options.explanation: Batch results are not guaranteed to come back in submission order; custom_id is what correlates each result to its request.

explanation: Correct: A. custom_id correlates requests and results, so the pipeline can resubmit only the failed items, fixed for the cause (chunking oversized inputs). Why not the others: B wastes cost on successes and the error is not transient; C repeats a deterministic failure; D relies on result order, which is not guaranteed.

prompt: A new contributor runs the team's review command locally before pushing, and it never mentions the error-handling conventions. The tech lead's local run on the same branch flags three violations of them. Both use the same Claude Code version and model. Which two steps best diagnose and fix the gap? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Reinstall Claude Code on the contributor's machine in case the local installation is damaged.
options.explanation: Both run the same version; nothing points to a broken install, and a reinstall would not add missing instructions.

options.text: Run /memory in both sessions to compare which memory files each one has actually loaded.
Switch the contributor to a larger model so it notices the error-handling conventions.
options.explanation: Both use the same model; the difference is in loaded instructions, which a different model would not supply.

options.text: Add the rules to the contributor's own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so their runs match the lead's.
options.explanation: This copies the problem: the rules stay out of version control and every future contributor and CI hits the same gap.

options.text: Move the rules from the lead's user-level file into the project CLAUDE.md under version control.

explanation: Correct: B and E. /memory shows which memory files a session loaded, which exposes instructions living in the lead's user-level file; moving them into the project CLAUDE.md shares them with everyone. Why not the others: A and C change things that are identical already; D spreads personal copies instead of fixing the shared configuration.

prompt: The bot left four comments on a PR: the session cache key omits the tenant ID, the cache TTL outlives the auth token, logout does not invalidate cached sessions, and a typo in README.md. The first three all live in `session_cache.py` and affect each other. How should the author hand these to Claude Code?

options.text: Send each cache issue as its own message, waiting for one fix before mentioning the next.
options.explanation: The cache issues interact, so fixing them one at a time invites a later fix to undo or conflict with an earlier one.

options.text: Paste all four comments, README typo included, and ask Claude to fix everything at once.
options.explanation: Bundling an unrelated change with the interacting ones muddies the request; independent issues are better handled separately.

options.text: Explain the three cache issues together in one detailed message; fix the README typo separately.
Fix only the tenant ID issue now and defer the other two cache issues to a later follow-up pull request.
options.explanation: Shipping one fix to code with interacting defects can leave the cache in an inconsistent state, and the deferred fixes may need to redo it.

explanation: Correct: C. Interacting issues are best described together in one detailed message so the fix accounts for all of them, while independent issues like the typo are handled on their own. Why not the others: A splits interacting issues; B mixes in an unrelated change; D ships a partial fix to coupled defects.

prompt: The root CLAUDE.md has grown to 1,200 lines: about 80 lines of coding standards (naming, error handling, logging) that matter on every review, and 1,100 lines of step-by-step instructions for drafting release-note comments, used once per release. Which two changes should the team make? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Keep the coding standards in CLAUDE.md, where they are loaded at the start of every session.
Move the coding standards into a skill so they load only when a developer asks for them.
options.explanation: Standards that apply to every review must always be present; making them on-demand means most runs would review without them.

options.text: Split the release procedure across subdirectory CLAUDE.md files spread throughout the tree.
options.explanation: The procedure is not tied to directories; scattering it would load fragments during unrelated work and never as one workflow.

options.text: Leave the file as it is, since every review the pipeline runs needs its full contents.
options.explanation: The release procedure is used once per release, so loading 1,100 lines on every review wastes context and dilutes attention.

options.text: Package the release-note procedure as a skill in .claude/skills/ and invoke it when needed.

explanation: Correct: A and E. CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded universal standards, while skills hold on-demand, task-specific workflows such as the release-note procedure. Why not the others: B hides standards that every review needs; C scatters a workflow by directory; D keeps loading a rarely used procedure on every run.

prompt: For small bug-fix PRs, the pipeline has Claude write a patch and tests, then in the same session asks "Review what you just wrote for problems." The self-review approves 95% of patches, yet humans later find defects in about one in six of them. Which two changes would most improve the review? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run the review in a separate instance that gets the patch but not the generator's conversation.
Add a verification pass that gives each finding a confidence level and routes low ones to a human.
Enable extended thinking in the generating session so its self-review reasons more deeply.
options.explanation: Longer reasoning in the same session still builds on the generator's own assumptions; an independent instance catches more.

options.text: Append "be critical of your own work" to the self-review request in the generating session.
options.explanation: An instruction to be critical does not remove the bias of reviewing one's own reasoning with that reasoning still in context.

options.text: Repeat the same self-review three times in that session and keep findings raised at least twice.
options.explanation: Repeated passes share the same context and blind spots, so they tend to agree with each other rather than surface new defects.

explanation: Correct: A and B. A model is less likely to question its own reasoning in the same session, so an independent instance without the generator's context reviews better; a verification pass with per-finding confidence routes uncertain cases to human review. Why not the others: C, D and E all keep the review inside the generating session with its blind spots.

prompt: Each finding in the output schema has `category` (enum: bug, security, performance) and a required string `suggested_fix`. Licensing problems and flaky-test risks are being forced into "bug", and when no safe fix is evident the model invents one that does not compile. Which two schema changes address this? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a prompt line telling the model to leave suggested_fix out whenever it is unsure of a fix.
options.explanation: The field is required, so omitting it fails validation; the schema and the instruction contradict each other.

options.text: Make suggested_fix nullable so the model can return null when no safe fix is evident.
Remove the category field entirely so the model is never forced to pick a wrong label.
options.explanation: Categories drive routing and dismissal analysis; dropping the field loses that structure instead of fixing the enum.

options.text: Add an enum value for every kind of issue the team has ever seen raised in a past review.
options.explanation: An ever-growing enum still breaks on the next new kind of issue and makes categories harder to choose between consistently.

options.text: Add "other" to the category enum together with a category_detail string describing it.

explanation: Correct: B and E. Nullable fields stop the model fabricating values the source cannot support, and an "other" enum value with a detail string keeps the schema extensible without forcing wrong labels. Why not the others: A conflicts with a required field; C throws away useful structure; D cannot anticipate every future case.

prompt: Yesterday a long review of PR #881 ran in a named session, `pr-881-review`. Overnight the author force-pushed a rewrite that changes 30 of the 34 files the session had read. The team wants an accurate second review without losing track of yesterday's conclusions. What should they do?

options.text: Resume pr-881-review with --resume and ask it to re-check the files it reviewed yesterday.
options.explanation: Resuming is for when prior context is mostly valid; here the session's tool results describe code that has largely been replaced.

options.text: Start a fresh session given a structured summary of yesterday's findings plus the current diff.
Resume the session and request a full new review, relying on its earlier tool results for context.
options.explanation: The earlier tool results are stale for 30 of 34 files, so leaning on them risks comments about code that no longer exists.

options.text: Use fork_session from pr-881-review so the new review branches off yesterday's analysis state.
options.explanation: Forking copies the same stale baseline; it is for comparing divergent approaches from a still-valid starting point.

explanation: Correct: B. When most prior tool results are stale, a fresh session seeded with a structured summary of earlier findings is more reliable than resuming; resuming fits when prior context is mostly valid. Why not the others: A and C carry outdated file contents; D branches from the same outdated state.

prompt: Since the pipeline switched to `--json-schema`, every response parses. Yet on some PRs the summary's `blocking_count` is 2 while three findings carry severity "blocking", and a few findings put the file path inside the `message` text instead of the `file` field. The lead says the schema should have caught this. What is the accurate response?

options.text: Tighten the schema with stricter string patterns until outputs like these can no longer validate.
options.explanation: Patterns cannot express that a count must equal the number of matching findings, and policing free text for paths is brittle.

options.text: A schema fixes syntax, not semantics; add a check that compares blocking_count with the findings.
Move blocking_count to the top of the schema so the model writes it before listing any findings.
options.explanation: Field order does not make the count consistent; written first, it is committed before the findings it should summarise exist.

options.text: Switch back from --json-schema to asking for JSON in the prompt, which gives the model more freedom.
options.explanation: That reintroduces parse failures while doing nothing for the semantic errors; schema-enforced output is the more reliable base.

explanation: Correct: B. Schema-constrained output removes syntax errors but not semantic ones such as totals that do not add up or values in the wrong field; those need programmatic checks and format rules in the prompt. Why not the others: A asks the schema to do semantic validation; C changes order, not correctness; D gives up syntax guarantees.

prompt: The prompt asks for a severity of critical, major or minor on each finding. An unchecked null dereference in the checkout flow was marked critical on Monday and minor on an almost identical PR on Thursday, and developers have started arguing with the labels. What should change?

options.text: Define each severity level with concrete code examples, e.g. a null deref in checkout as critical.
Tell the reviewer to "assign severity carefully and consistently", prefixed with IMPORTANT.
options.explanation: Emphasis adds urgency but no definition, so the model still has to guess where the boundary between levels lies.

options.text: Drop severity from the output and let developers judge the importance of each comment.
options.explanation: Severity helps prioritise and route findings; removing it hides the inconsistency rather than fixing the criteria.

options.text: Let the reviewer pick severity freely, then remap it afterwards by counting alarming words in the text.
options.explanation: Word counting measures tone, not impact, and adds a second unreliable step on top of undefined levels.

explanation: Correct: A. Severity criteria backed by concrete code examples for each level give the model a fixed reference, so the same defect gets the same label across PRs. Why not the others: B adds emphasis without definitions; C removes useful prioritisation; D derives severity from wording rather than impact.

prompt: Some suppliers print several dates on an invoice: "Invoice date", "Tax point", "Dispatch date" and sometimes "Date of supply". The schema has one `invoice_date` field, and the prompt says "use the invoice date". Reviewers see the model pick different dates on similar documents, and they disagree with its choice about a quarter of the time when there is no label literally reading "Invoice date". What should the team add to the prompt?

options.text: A longer list of every date label suppliers might use, so the model can look up which label maps to the field.
options.explanation: A label list does not convey the decision rule for conflicting dates and will miss labels not yet seen.

options.text: An instruction to return the earliest date found on the document, which is easy to apply consistently.
options.explanation: A consistent but wrong rule: the earliest date is often a dispatch or order date, not the invoice date.

options.text: Two to four examples of multi-date invoices showing which date was chosen and the reasoning for that choice.
A request to put every date found into `invoice_date` as a comma-separated list for downstream code to resolve.
options.explanation: This breaks the field's type and pushes the ambiguity onto downstream systems that lack the context to resolve it.

explanation: Correct: C. Few-shot examples that show how ambiguous cases are handled, and why one option was chosen over plausible alternatives, give the model a judgement it can generalise to new layouts. Why not the others: A lists labels without conveying the decision; B applies a simple but incorrect rule; D abandons the schema and moves the problem downstream.

prompt: A newly written prompt for lease agreements has been tested on a dozen hand-picked leases and looks good. The team now wants to run it over 120,000 archived leases in one go using the Message Batches API to populate a new lease register. What should happen before the full submission?

options.text: Run the prompt on a representative sample of a few hundred leases, review the output, and refine it before batching.
Submit the full set now, because the 50% batch discount makes a second full run cheap if the results disappoint.
options.explanation: Even at half price, rerunning 120,000 documents wastes cost and up to a day per pass on problems a sample would reveal.

options.text: Split the archive into 12 batches of 10,000 and submit them together so any failures are spread across batches.
options.explanation: Splitting does not test the prompt; the same flaws would appear in every batch.

options.text: Process the archive synchronously at full price instead, so that errors show up immediately as each lease is extracted.
options.explanation: This doubles the cost without first validating the prompt; refining on a sample is the efficient step.

explanation: Correct: A. Refining the prompt on a representative sample before batching large volumes catches problems cheaply; a dozen hand-picked leases is not representative. Why not the others: B wastes a full run that a sample would have prevented; C partitions the work without validating the prompt; D pays full price and still skips prompt validation.

prompt: On roughly 2% of invoices, the printed total differs from the sum of the line items, usually because a supplier forgot a line or applied a discount without listing it. Reviewers found that the model quietly reports whichever figure seems more plausible, so neither the discrepancy nor its choice is visible downstream. Which schema change best handles this?

options.text: Tell the model to recompute `total` from the line items whenever the two disagree, since arithmetic is more reliable.
options.explanation: Overwriting the printed total hides a real discrepancy, such as an unlisted discount, that accounts payable needs to see.

options.text: Add `stated_total`, `calculated_total` and a `conflict_detected` boolean, and route records with a detected conflict to review.
Keep one `total` field and add a JSON schema rule requiring it to equal the sum of the line-item amounts.
options.explanation: Standard JSON schema cannot express cross-field sums, and forcing equality would push the model to alter one of the figures.

options.text: Instruct the model to trust the printed total, since it is what the supplier legally invoiced, and drop the line items.
options.explanation: Dropping line items discards data downstream systems need and still hides the discrepancy.

explanation: Correct: B. Self-check fields such as a calculated total alongside the stated total, plus a `conflict_detected` flag, make inconsistencies explicit so they can be routed rather than silently resolved. Why not the others: A and D each pick one figure and hide the conflict; C asks the schema to enforce a semantic rule it cannot express and would encourage the model to alter data.

prompt: For each supplier, the pipeline builds one record from a master contract, its latest amendment and recent invoices. For Brightwell Chemicals, the 2024 contract gives payment terms of net 30, a March 2026 amendment says net 45, and the October invoice prints "Payment due in 60 days". Which two behaviours should the pipeline have? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use the value from the most recently dated document, the invoice, because later documents supersede earlier ones.
options.explanation: An invoice does not amend contract terms; picking by date silently hides a genuine discrepancy.

options.text: Record each value with its source document, date and quoted excerpt, so the conflict and its origins stay visible.
Treat the master contract as authoritative and discard the other values so the record stays clean for loading.
options.explanation: This ignores a valid amendment and drops evidence of the invoice discrepancy.

options.text: Set a conflict flag on the record and route it to a human reviewer instead of letting the model resolve it.
Ask the model to decide which source is most credible and write only that value, noting its reasoning in a log.
options.explanation: Letting the model pick one value for contradictory sources is guessing; the output loses the alternatives downstream.

explanation: Correct: B and D. Conflicting values from credible sources should be kept with attribution (document, date, excerpt) rather than reduced to one, and ambiguous or contradictory sources should be routed to human review. Why not the others: A and C apply fixed precedence rules that hide a real conflict; E has the model silently pick one value.

prompt: The schema types `issue_date` as a string with pattern `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` and `amount` as a number. Outputs pass validation, yet reconciliation finds that "04/05/2026" on a Lyon supplier's invoice became 2026-04-05, and "1.250" from a German supplier became 1.25 instead of 1250. What should the team add?

options.text: A stricter schema with separate `day`, `month` and `year` integer fields, so dates cannot be stored in the wrong order.
options.explanation: Splitting the date still leaves the model to decide which number is the day; the locale rule is missing, not the structure.

options.text: Prompt rules for normalising values, such as reading dates and decimal marks by supplier country, alongside the schema.
A validator that rejects any date whose day value is 12 or lower, forcing a retry for each potentially ambiguous date.
options.explanation: Retries without a rule just repeat the same guess, and many valid dates would be rejected for no reason.

options.text: A post-processing script that converts every date and amount using US conventions, since the ledger runs in USD.
options.explanation: Applying one locale's conventions to European documents reproduces exactly the errors observed.

explanation: Correct: B. A strict schema fixes the output format, but the model also needs explicit normalisation rules, such as how to interpret dates and number separators by locale, to fill those fields correctly. Why not the others: A changes structure without the interpretation rule; C rejects valid data and retries blindly; D imposes the wrong conventions on European suppliers.

prompt: To assign GL codes, the agent needs the chart of accounts (about 900 codes with descriptions) and the list of active cost centres. Traces show it making 15 to 25 calls to `search_accounts` per invoice, trying keywords like "freight", "logistics" and "shipping" until something matches. The data changes about once a month. What change would most reduce these exploratory calls?

options.text: Expose the chart of accounts and cost centres as MCP resources that the agent can read as a catalog instead of searching.
Raise the `search_accounts` page size so each call returns up to 200 matching accounts rather than the current 20.
options.explanation: Larger pages still depend on keyword guessing and flood the context with irrelevant accounts.

options.text: Cap the agent at five `search_accounts` calls per invoice and send the invoice to review if no code is found by then.
options.explanation: A cap cuts calls by abandoning work, raising review volume, without giving the agent the data it needs.

options.text: Add to the system prompt that the agent should think harder about which keyword to search with before each call.
options.explanation: Better guessing still means exploring blind; the agent lacks a view of what accounts exist.

explanation: Correct: A. MCP resources expose content catalogs, such as reference data or schemas, so the agent can see what exists without repeated exploratory tool calls; slowly changing reference data suits this well. Why not the others: B makes each blind search noisier; C trades calls for more manual review; D leaves the agent guessing keywords.

prompt: Human reviewers currently look only at extractions with low confidence or a validation warning; the remaining 88% load automatically. Nobody knows the error rate in that auto-loaded share, and a recent audit found a new failure: credit notes from one supplier loaded as positive invoices, all with high confidence. How should the team monitor the auto-loaded records?

options.text: Review the auto-loaded records only when downstream reconciliation reports a mismatch at month end.
options.explanation: Waiting for reconciliation detects errors late and only those that happen to break a total.

options.text: Lower the confidence threshold so that more records fall into the existing low-confidence review queue.
options.explanation: This adds review load but still never looks at high-confidence records, where this failure lived.

options.text: Review a stratified random sample of high-confidence records, split by document type and supplier.
Ask the model to double-check its high-confidence extractions in a second turn before they are loaded.
options.explanation: Self-review in the same context rarely catches its own errors and gives no measured error rate.

explanation: Correct: C. Stratified random sampling of high-confidence extractions measures the true error rate in the automated share and surfaces novel failure patterns like this one. Why not the others: A detects only errors that break reconciliation, and late; B still skips high-confidence records; D relies on self-review and produces no measurement.

prompt: The extractor emits a confidence value per field, and records above 0.9 skip review. A labelled audit of 2,000 documents shows `supplier_name` above 0.9 is wrong 0.4% of the time, but `tax_amount` above 0.9 is wrong 11% of the time, mostly on multi-rate invoices. How should routing be changed?

options.text: Raise the single threshold to 0.97 for every field, so that fewer uncertain values of any kind skip review.
options.explanation: One threshold ignores that confidence means different things per field; it over-reviews reliable fields and may still pass bad tax amounts.

options.text: Remove the confidence values and send every record to review until the model produces better calibrated output.
options.explanation: This discards a useful signal for fields like `supplier_name` that already perform well.

options.text: Add a prompt instruction telling the model to report lower confidence for tax amounts on invoices with multiple rates.
options.explanation: Asking the model to adjust its own scores does not calibrate them against measured accuracy.

options.text: Calibrate each field's threshold on a labelled validation set and route fields below it to review.

explanation: Correct: D. Field-level confidence should be calibrated on labelled validation data so each field's threshold reflects its measured error rate; low-confidence fields then go to humans. Why not the others: A applies one threshold to fields that behave differently; B throws away a working signal; C asks the model to tune its own scores without calibration.

prompt: Last night's batch of 50,000 statements finished with 1,140 errored requests. The error details show all of them exceeded the context window; each is a statement over 400 pages from three custodian banks. The other 48,860 results are loaded. What should the team do next?

options.text: Resubmit the whole batch of 50,000 tonight with a shorter system prompt to free up room for the large statements.
options.explanation: This reprocesses 48,860 good results and a shorter prompt will not make 400-page documents fit.

options.text: Resubmit the same 1,140 requests unchanged, since batch errors are often transient and clear up on a second run.
options.explanation: Context-length errors are deterministic; the same oversized requests will fail again.

options.text: Chunk the oversized statements and resubmit only those requests by `custom_id`, then merge the chunk results.
Move the three custodian banks to synchronous calls permanently, since batches cannot handle large documents.
options.explanation: The size limit applies to synchronous calls too; the documents need chunking either way.

explanation: Correct: C. The right recovery is to fix the cause (chunk oversized documents) and resubmit only the failed requests, identified by `custom_id`, leaving successful results untouched. Why not the others: A reruns successful work without fixing the cause; B repeats a deterministic failure; D misattributes the limit to batching when it is the context window.

prompt: Master supply agreements run 70 to 120 pages. The extractor reliably captures parties and pricing (near the start) and governing law and signatures (near the end), but misses termination-for-convenience and liability-cap clauses in pages 40 to 80 about a third of the time. What change best addresses this?

options.text: Summarise the agreement first in a separate call, then run the extraction on the summary, which fits more easily.
options.explanation: Summaries tend to drop specific figures and clause details, the very content being missed.

options.text: Add "Read the entire document carefully, including the middle sections" to the top of the system prompt.
options.explanation: Exhortation does not change how attention is spread over a very long input.

options.text: Raise `max_tokens` on the request so the model has enough output budget to cover every clause in the agreement.
options.explanation: Output budget is not the issue; the clauses are missed while reading, not cut off while writing.

options.text: Extract clause fields section by section in separate passes, then merge them in a consolidation pass.

explanation: Correct: D. Content in the middle of long inputs is processed less reliably than the start and end; splitting the agreement into section-sized passes puts each clause near the edges of its own input, and a consolidation pass assembles the record. Why not the others: A loses detail through summarisation; B is an exhortation with no mechanism; C changes output length, not reading.

prompt: The extractor also raises anomaly findings in five categories. Reviewers report that "unusual supplier address" findings are wrong 85% of the time, while "duplicate invoice number" findings are almost always right, yet they have started dismissing both without reading. Which two changes should the team make? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add "Only raise findings you are very sure about" to the prompt for all five categories.
options.explanation: Confidence wording does not raise precision the way concrete criteria do, and it may suppress accurate findings.

options.text: Move the anomaly instructions to the very end of the prompt so the model weights them more heavily than the rest.
options.explanation: Repositioning instructions does not define what counts as a real address anomaly.

options.text: Temporarily disable the address category while its criteria are rewritten, keeping the accurate ones running.
Define each category with concrete report and skip conditions, such as ignoring suite or postcode format changes.
Raise `max_tokens` so the model can write a longer justification under each anomaly it reports to reviewers.
options.explanation: Longer justifications add reading load without making the address findings any more accurate.

explanation: Correct: C and D. A high false-positive category erodes trust in accurate ones, so disabling it temporarily restores trust while its prompt is fixed, and explicit categorical report/skip criteria are what improve precision. Why not the others: A relies on confidence wording that does not improve precision; B moves instructions without defining them; E lengthens output without making findings more accurate.

prompt: Reviewers dismiss about 40% of the pipeline's "possible duplicate payment" findings, but the dismissal log records only accept or dismiss. The team wants to learn which situations produce the bad findings so it can fix the prompt with evidence rather than guesses. What should it add?

options.text: A `detected_pattern` field naming what triggered each finding, so dismissals can be grouped by pattern.
A free-text comment box where reviewers can explain each dismissal in their own words if they have time.
options.explanation: Optional free text is sparse and inconsistent, making systematic analysis of triggers difficult.

options.text: A model-reported confidence score on each finding, so low-scoring findings can be hidden from reviewers.
options.explanation: Hiding findings by uncalibrated score does not reveal which situations cause the false positives.

options.text: A monthly rerun of dismissed findings through the same prompt to see whether the model still raises them.
options.explanation: Rerunning the same prompt reproduces the same findings and explains nothing about their causes.

explanation: Correct: A. Adding a `detected_pattern` field to each finding records what triggered it, so dismissal rates can be analysed per pattern and the prompt fixed where the evidence points. Why not the others: B yields sparse, unstructured data; C hides findings without diagnosing them; D repeats the same behaviour without insight.

prompt: For three-way matching, a coordinator sends each payment packet (purchase order, goods receipt, invoice) to an extraction subagent. For packet PKT-20417, the OCR service times out twice on the goods receipt; the purchase order and invoice extract cleanly. Which two behaviours should the subagent and coordinator show? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The subagent returns the goods receipt as an empty object marked success, so the coordinator can carry on with matching.
options.explanation: Returning an access failure as an empty success makes it look like the receipt has no lines, corrupting the match.

options.text: The subagent reports a structured error naming the failure type, the document attempted, retries made and the partial results.
The coordinator aborts the entire nightly matching run so that no packet is matched while any document is unreadable.
options.explanation: Aborting the whole workflow on one failure throws away every good result.

options.text: The coordinator marks the packet's match as incomplete, noting the missing receipt, and queues it for retry or review.
The subagent keeps retrying the OCR call until it succeeds, holding the packet open for as long as that takes.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries stall the packet and the run; after local retries the error should be propagated with context.

explanation: Correct: B and D. Subagents should recover locally where they can and then propagate structured error context, including failure type, what was attempted and partial results, so the coordinator can mark the gap and route the packet for recovery. Why not the others: A disguises an access failure as a valid empty result; C aborts everything for one failure; E retries without limit instead of escalating.

prompt: The contract extractor sets `nonstandard_clause: true` when a clause departs from the group's standard terms. Legal finds it inconsistent: a mutual auto-renewal with 90 days' notice is flagged in one contract and not another, while a one-sided indemnity is sometimes missed. Instructions describing the standard terms in prose have not helped. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Add a few examples contrasting acceptable variants with true deviations, each with a brief reason.
Expand the prose with a full list of every acceptable clause wording that legal has approved so far.
options.explanation: An exhaustive wording list cannot cover new phrasings and does not teach where the line between acceptable and deviant lies.

options.text: Ask the model to flag any clause it is unsure about, so that legal sees everything that could be a deviation.
options.explanation: Flagging all uncertainty floods legal with false positives and does not make the judgement more consistent.

options.text: Replace the boolean with a 1 to 10 deviation score so legal can choose its own cut-off for what to review.
options.explanation: A score moves the inconsistency into a number; without a clearer standard the scores will vary just as much.

explanation: Correct: A. When prose instructions produce inconsistent judgements, targeted few-shot examples that distinguish acceptable patterns from real issues, with reasoning, teach the model a judgement that generalises. Why not the others: B tries to enumerate wording and will not generalise; C trades consistency for noise; D relabels the same inconsistent judgement as a score.

prompt: The `currency` field is an enum of `USD`, `CAD`, `AUD`, `EUR` and `GBP`. Some invoices show only a "$" sign with no country, address or currency code anywhere on the page. Audits find the model picks `USD` for these, and about a fifth of them are actually Canadian or Australian. How should the schema handle these documents?

options.text: Default `currency` to `USD` in the schema, since most dollar-sign invoices are in US dollars and the rest are rare.
options.explanation: A default makes the guess official; a fifth of these invoices would still be booked in the wrong currency.

options.text: Add an `unclear` enum value for cases the document cannot settle, and route those records to a reviewer.
Remove the enum and make `currency` a free-text string so the model can write whatever the document shows.
options.explanation: Free text loses validation and downstream consistency, and "$" still does not say which currency it is.

options.text: Add a prompt rule to infer the currency from the supplier's typical pricing levels when no code is printed.
options.explanation: Inferring from price levels is guessing; the document does not support a confident answer.

explanation: Correct: B. An `unclear` enum value lets the model report genuine ambiguity instead of forcing a guess, and those records can be routed for human resolution. Why not the others: A institutionalises the wrong guess; C gives up validation without resolving the ambiguity; D replaces evidence with inference.

prompt: A freight brokerage is building a quoting agent directly on the Claude API, with tools `get_lane_rates` and `check_carrier_capacity`. The engineer is writing the loop that decides whether to call Claude again or return a quote to the shipper. Which two loop behaviours are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Exit the loop once the assistant text contains a phrase such as 'quote complete', which the prompt tells Claude to say
options.explanation: Parsing natural-language text to decide termination is a named anti-pattern; the phrase can appear alongside a pending tool call or not appear at all.

options.text: When stop_reason is 'tool_use', run each requested tool and append its tool_result to the history before the next request
Treat stop_reason 'end_turn' as the signal to leave the loop and hand the final assistant response back to the caller
Set a cap of three iterations as the main exit condition, so each quote request finishes in a predictable time
options.explanation: An arbitrary iteration cap as the primary stop cuts off quotes that legitimately need more tool calls; a cap is a safety net, not the exit rule.

options.text: Send just the latest tool_result on each request instead of the whole history, keeping the tokens per call flat
options.explanation: The API is stateless: the full conversation, including earlier tool calls and results, must be sent each time or Claude loses what it already learned.

explanation: Correct: B and C. The loop is driven by stop_reason: 'tool_use' means execute the requested tools and append their results to the history, and 'end_turn' means Claude has finished. Why not the others: A decides termination by parsing assistant text; D makes an arbitrary cap the primary stop; E drops the history that each stateless request needs.

prompt: A hotel chain's revenue-management agent logged a response containing a text block, "I have everything I need, finalising the price recommendation now", followed by a `tool_use` block for `get_competitor_rates`, with `stop_reason: "tool_use"`. The loop exited because the text matched the phrase 'everything I need', and the recommendation shipped without competitor data. What is the right fix?

options.text: Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude not to announce completion until the final answer is fully written
options.explanation: This keeps termination tied to parsing the model's wording, which stays unreliable however carefully the prompt is phrased.

options.text: Require at least two iterations before the loop may exit, so it cannot stop on the first response it receives
options.explanation: A minimum iteration count is as arbitrary as a maximum; the same bug reappears whenever the phrase shows up on a later turn.

options.text: Strip text blocks from any response that also has a tool_use block, so the completion phrase is not seen by the loop
options.explanation: Hiding text treats the symptom; the loop would still be deciding termination from text rather than from the structured stop signal.

options.text: Base termination on stop_reason: execute the tool when it is 'tool_use', and exit the loop once it is 'end_turn'

explanation: Correct: D. stop_reason is the structured signal for loop control; 'tool_use' means a tool call is pending and must be executed and its result appended before Claude continues. Why not the others: A still relies on parsing natural language; B swaps one arbitrary count for another; C hides the text but keeps text-driven termination.

prompt: A geological survey firm's agent interprets well-log files with tools for curve lookup and lithology classification. A few runs loop more than 40 times on noisy files. An engineer proposes making `max_iterations=8` the loop's exit condition. Which design should the architect choose?

options.text: Keep stop_reason as the exit condition and add a generous cap as a safety net that logs any run hitting it
Make the cap of 8 the main exit, since a fixed budget gives each well-log analysis a predictable cost and runtime
options.explanation: Using the cap as the primary stop truncates complex files mid-analysis and returns incomplete interpretations as if they were finished.

options.text: Exit once two consecutive responses contain no new numbers in their text, which shows that the analysis has converged
options.explanation: This invents a text heuristic for termination; numbers in prose are not a reliable signal that Claude has finished its tool work.

options.text: Ask Claude to put a JSON field done:true in its text and end the loop whenever that field appears in a response
options.explanation: A self-reported flag in assistant text is still parsing output to decide termination, which the stop_reason field already handles.

explanation: Correct: A. The loop should end when stop_reason is 'end_turn'; a cap remains useful as a guard against runaway loops, but hitting it is an anomaly to surface, not a normal exit. Why not the others: B makes an arbitrary cap the primary stop; C and D both decide termination by parsing assistant text instead of the structured signal.

prompt: A city permits office runs an Agent SDK coordinator with four subagents: zoning lookup, document analysis, precedent search and report writing. A clerk's question like "Is permit 4471 approved?" passes through all four and takes 90 seconds. Complex variance requests do need the full chain. What should change?

options.text: Merge the four subagents into a single agent holding the combined toolset, removing delegation overhead for each query
options.explanation: One agent with every tool brings back tool-selection problems and loses context isolation; the complex requests still benefit from specialists.

options.text: Have the coordinator judge each request's complexity and invoke just the subagents that request actually needs
Run the four subagents in parallel for each request, so the full pipeline returns faster on simple status lookups
options.explanation: Parallelism trims latency but still spends four subagents on a one-step lookup; the issue is invoking agents the query does not need.

options.text: Put a keyword router in front of the coordinator that sends any message with a permit number straight to report writing
options.explanation: A brittle keyword rule bypasses the coordinator's judgement; complex variance requests also mention permit numbers and would be misrouted.

explanation: Correct: B. In hub-and-spoke designs the coordinator picks which subagents to invoke based on the query, rather than pushing every request through the full pipeline. Why not the others: A collapses specialists into one overloaded agent; C still runs unnecessary subagents; D replaces coordinator judgement with a fragile keyword rule.

prompt: A pharmaceutical safety team asked its research coordinator about "adverse cardiac events linked to compound RX-17". The coordinator delegated three tasks: QT prolongation in trials, QT prolongation in case reports, and QT prolongation in meta-analyses. The final report says nothing about the heart-failure and arrhythmia signals that reviewers later found in the literature. What is the root cause?

options.text: The synthesis subagent's context window was too small to hold three separate sets of subagent findings
options.explanation: Three focused result sets are small; and the missing events were never searched for, so no synthesis budget could surface them.

options.text: The subagents had no shared memory store, so none of them could see what the others had already found
options.explanation: Subagents are meant to be isolated; shared memory would not add topics the coordinator never assigned to anyone.

options.text: The coordinator's decomposition was too narrow, leaving cardiac events other than QT prolongation unassigned
The search subagents returned too many results, so relevance ranking quietly dropped the rarer cardiac events
options.explanation: Nothing suggests ranking dropped results; all three tasks were scoped to QT prolongation, so other events were outside every query.

explanation: Correct: C. Overly narrow decomposition is a named coverage risk: the coordinator partitioned one subtopic by source type and never assigned the other cardiac events. Why not the others: A blames context size for gaps that were never searched; B asks for shared memory when subagents should be isolated; D invents a ranking problem the task scopes do not support.

prompt: In an insurer's claims system, a fraud-signal subagent sends its findings straight to the payout-calculation subagent over a shared queue, bypassing the coordinator. Last week the fraud subagent timed out on 31 claims; payouts went ahead without any fraud check and nothing in the coordinator's logs showed the gap. What change best addresses this?

options.text: Add retries inside the shared queue, so the payout subagent waits until a fraud message eventually arrives
options.explanation: Waiting on the queue hides the failure in a different place; nobody owns the decision of what to do when the fraud check cannot complete.

options.text: Route inter-subagent results through the coordinator, which tracks each and handles errors consistently
Give the payout subagent the fraud-detection tools too, so it can recompute any missing signal by itself
options.explanation: This blurs role boundaries and adds out-of-role tools; the coordinator still has no visibility into what ran or failed.

options.text: Have each subagent write its output to a shared log file that the payout subagent polls before running
options.explanation: A shared file is another side channel; it does not give the coordinator observability or a single place to handle errors.

explanation: Correct: B. The coordinator should handle inter-subagent communication so it can observe each step, notice a missing fraud result and apply one error-handling policy. Why not the others: A and D keep a side channel the coordinator cannot see; C gives a subagent out-of-role tools instead of fixing the routing.

prompt: An energy-market research firm's coordinator receives a synthesised report on battery storage. The section on grid-scale pricing after 2024 rests on a single source, while other sections cite six or more. The report is due tomorrow. What should the coordinator do next?

options.text: Ask the synthesis subagent to expand the thin section using its own background knowledge of battery pricing
options.explanation: Filling gaps from model knowledge produces unsourced claims in a cited report; the gap needs new evidence, not more prose.

options.text: Identify the gap, delegate a targeted search for post-2024 grid-scale pricing, then re-run synthesis
Re-run the entire pipeline from the start with the same decomposition, giving each subagent a second pass
options.explanation: Repeating the same decomposition likely reproduces the same thin coverage and wastes the work that is already adequate.

options.text: Publish the report as it stands, since the synthesis subagent already judged which findings were well supported
options.explanation: The coordinator owns quality checks; shipping a known gap without annotation or follow-up skips the refinement step.

explanation: Correct: B. Iterative refinement means the coordinator evaluates the synthesis for gaps, re-delegates targeted queries for them, and re-runs synthesis. Why not the others: A adds unsourced content; C redoes everything rather than targeting the gap; D skips the coordinator's quality check.

prompt: A logistics company's Agent SDK coordinator has three subagents defined for route, customs and carrier analysis. Logs show it never delegates; it attempts every task itself and once replied that it has no way to start helpers. Its options include `allowedTools: ["Read", "Grep", "WebSearch"]`. What is the most likely fix?

options.text: Add a sentence to the coordinator's system prompt telling it to delegate shipment analysis to its subagents
options.explanation: The coordinator cannot follow that instruction: without the Task tool in its allowed tools it has no means of spawning a subagent.

options.text: Give each subagent definition the same allowedTools list as the coordinator, so that their scopes line up
options.explanation: Subagent tool lists control what each subagent may do once spawned; they do not give the coordinator the ability to spawn them.

options.text: Add 'Task' to the coordinator's allowedTools, since subagents are spawned through calls to the Task tool
Set tool_choice to 'any' on the coordinator, so that it is required to call some tool on each of its turns
options.explanation: Forcing a tool call only makes it pick among Read, Grep and WebSearch; none of them can start a subagent.

explanation: Correct: C. Subagents are invoked through the Task tool, so the coordinator's allowedTools must include 'Task' before it can delegate. Why not the others: A asks for behaviour the coordinator has no tool for; B changes subagent scopes rather than the coordinator's; D forces a call among tools that cannot delegate.

prompt: An agritech company defines two subagent types with `AgentDefinition`: a soil analyst that may write to the soil database and a weather forecaster that should be read-only. The coordinator is told about a field's sensor readings at the start of each run. Which two statements about this setup are correct? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Each subagent receives the coordinator's conversation so far, so the sensor readings need not be repeated in its prompt
options.explanation: Subagents start with isolated context and do not inherit the coordinator's history; the readings must be passed in the prompt explicitly.

options.text: Subagents defined this way share one context window with the coordinator, which keeps their findings visible to each other
options.explanation: Each subagent runs in its own context; findings move between agents only through what the coordinator passes and receives.

options.text: The description field tells the coordinator what each subagent type is for, which guides when it chooses to invoke it
A per-type tools list can restrict the forecaster to forecast tools, keeping soil-database writes out of its reach
A subagent's system prompt is inherited from the coordinator, so per-type instructions have to go in each Task call
options.explanation: AgentDefinition carries its own system prompt for the subagent type; that is where per-type instructions belong.

explanation: Correct: C and D. An AgentDefinition gives each subagent type a description (used to decide when to invoke it), its own system prompt and its own tool restrictions. Why not the others: A and B assume shared history or context, but subagents are isolated and need context passed explicitly; E is wrong because the definition carries its own system prompt.

prompt: A security operations team's coordinator checks a suspicious IP address against three threat-intelligence feeds, one subagent per feed. Traces show the coordinator emits one Task call, waits for its result, then emits the next Task call on its following turn, so a check takes three times as long as the slowest feed. How should this be fixed?

options.text: Have each subagent call the next one when it finishes, so the chain continues without the coordinator waiting on it
options.explanation: Chaining subagents bypasses the coordinator, removing its view of results and errors, and the calls still run one after another.

options.text: Prompt the coordinator to issue the three Task calls together in one response, so the subagents run in parallel
Merge the three feeds into one subagent holding the three tools, so a single Task call covers the lookups
options.explanation: One subagent still performs the lookups in its own sequence and loses the per-feed isolation; it does not create parallelism.

options.text: Lower the coordinator's max_tokens, so each of its turns completes sooner and the three turns take less time
options.explanation: The delay comes from waiting on each subagent in turn, not from coordinator output length; shorter turns barely change it.

explanation: Correct: B. Parallel subagents are spawned by emitting multiple Task calls in a single coordinator response; issuing them across separate turns serialises the work. Why not the others: A bypasses the coordinator and stays sequential; C removes isolation without parallelism; D targets output length rather than the serial waits.

prompt: In a legal-tech contract review system, a clause-extraction subagent returns 14 indemnity and liability clauses to the coordinator. The coordinator then spawns a risk-scoring subagent with the prompt "Score the risks in the clauses we found." The scorer returns generic advice about indemnity clauses. What should change?

options.text: Give the risk scorer read access to the coordinator's session transcript, so it can locate the clauses by itself
options.explanation: Subagents do not share the coordinator's memory; exposing a transcript is a workaround that buries the clauses in unrelated turns.

options.text: Pass the clauses in the scorer's prompt as structured items, with clause text kept apart from contract and page
Tell the scorer to message the coordinator mid-task whenever it needs the clause text for a particular contract
options.explanation: Subagents run with what their prompt gives them and return a result; they cannot hold a conversation with the coordinator mid-task.

options.text: Shorten the prompt to the clause numbers, so the scorer can retrieve each clause's wording from its own memory
options.explanation: The scorer has no memory of the extraction; clause numbers alone give it nothing to score.

explanation: Correct: B. Subagent context must be passed explicitly in the prompt, including complete prior findings, and a structured format that separates content from metadata keeps attribution intact. Why not the others: A relies on shared memory that does not exist; C assumes mid-task conversation; D strips out the content the scorer needs.

prompt: A news organisation's fact-checking coordinator writes a 25-step procedure into each subagent prompt ("search the wire archive, open the top three hits, then..."). When step 2 returns nothing, subagents keep following the steps and miss better sources such as court records. How should the coordinator's prompts be rewritten?

options.text: State the claim, what counts as adequate evidence and the output required, leaving search steps to the subagent
Add branches to the procedure so that each subagent has a defined next step for any search that comes back empty
options.explanation: More branches make the script longer and more brittle; the subagent still cannot adapt to situations the author did not foresee.

options.text: Move the procedure into the coordinator, which runs the searches itself and passes raw results to subagents
options.explanation: This turns subagents into formatters and puts verbose search work back into the coordinator's context.

options.text: Keep the procedure but add 'use your judgement' at the end, so subagents can deviate whenever a step fails
options.explanation: A vague escape clause on top of a rigid script gives no criteria for when or how to deviate.

explanation: Correct: A. Coordinator prompts should specify goals and quality criteria rather than step-by-step procedures, so subagents can choose how to reach the goal. Why not the others: B makes the script more rigid; C pulls the work back into the coordinator; D adds vague licence without criteria.

prompt: A payroll platform's agent can call `run_payroll_adjustment`. Policy requires `approve_manager_signoff` to return an approval first, and the system prompt states this clearly with examples. An audit found 2 of 1,300 adjustments executed with no sign-off on record. What should the team do?

options.text: Move the sign-off rule to the top of the system prompt and repeat it at the end, to counter lost-in-the-middle effects
options.explanation: Rewording or repositioning the prompt can reduce the rate but cannot make a probabilistic instruction deterministic.

options.text: Add more few-shot examples that show the agent getting sign-off before each adjustment it performs
options.explanation: Examples already exist; more of them still leave a non-zero failure rate where the policy demands none.

options.text: Have the agent state in its reasoning that sign-off was obtained before it calls the adjustment tool
options.explanation: A self-attestation is generated by the same model that skipped the step; it does not check anything.

options.text: Add a programmatic gate that blocks run_payroll_adjustment until sign-off has returned an approval for that employee

explanation: Correct: D. When compliance must be deterministic, prompt instructions alone have a non-zero failure rate; a prerequisite gate in code blocks the call until the required step has succeeded. Why not the others: A and B tune a probabilistic control; C asks the model to vouch for itself without any check.

prompt: A telecom's network-repair agent escalates unresolved outage cases to a human dispatcher. The dispatcher works from a queue view and never sees the agent's conversation with the customer. Which two items should the structured handoff include? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The raw transcript in place of a summary, so the dispatcher can reread the whole conversation for themselves
options.explanation: Dumping the transcript makes the dispatcher re-derive the diagnosis; the handoff should state the conclusions in structured fields.

options.text: The agent's self-reported confidence score, used as the main signal of how urgent the case is
options.explanation: Self-reported confidence is a poor proxy for urgency or complexity and tells the dispatcher nothing about what to do.

options.text: The site and account identifiers, along with the diagnosed root cause and the evidence behind it
The recommended next action, such as a truck roll to cabinet 12, with any service credit already calculated
A one-line note reading 'customer issue unresolved, please review', so the dispatcher's queue stays short
options.explanation: A bare note forces the dispatcher to start over because it omits identifiers, cause and recommended action.

explanation: Correct: C and D. Humans receiving an escalation lack the transcript, so the handoff should carry identifiers, root cause, amounts and the recommended action in a structured form. Why not the others: A hands over raw text instead of conclusions; B relies on an unreliable confidence signal; E omits the facts needed to act.

prompt: A property-management assistant receives one tenant message reporting a leaking boiler, disputing a late fee, and asking whether the lease can be renewed for 18 months. The current agent fixes the boiler ticket and its reply ignores the other two points. Which workflow should replace it?

options.text: Answer the first concern now and ask the tenant to send the other two as separate messages later
options.explanation: Pushing the decomposition onto the tenant degrades the experience and loses the shared context of one message.

options.text: Route the message to the specialist agent for the most urgent concern and let that agent handle the rest
options.explanation: A single specialist is scoped to one area and is likely to repeat the same failure on the concerns outside its role.

options.text: Split it into three items, investigate them in parallel with shared tenant context, and send one combined reply
Work through the three concerns in separate sessions, one after another, so that no investigation sees the others
options.explanation: Isolating them discards the shared tenant context and serialises work that could run in parallel.

explanation: Correct: C. Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, investigated in parallel using shared context, and synthesised into one resolution. Why not the others: A offloads the work to the tenant; B gives one specialist concerns outside its scope; D drops shared context and parallelism.

prompt: An airline maintenance agent pulls records from three MCP servers. One returns Unix epoch timestamps, one returns ISO 8601 strings, and one reports component status as numeric codes (0, 1, 2) where the others use words like 'serviceable'. The agent has misordered inspection events and misread statuses. Which two changes give a deterministic fix? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Add a table to the system prompt describing each server's timestamp format and code meanings for the model to apply
options.explanation: Asking the model to convert formats is probabilistic; it can still slip, which is the failure being seen now.

options.text: Use a PostToolUse hook to convert all timestamps to ISO 8601 before the model sees any of the results
Map the numeric status codes to named statuses in the same hook, so each result uses one vocabulary
Use a pre-call hook to block calls to the epoch-timestamp server until its vendor changes the format
options.explanation: Blocking the server removes needed maintenance data; pre-call hooks gate calls, while the problem is in the results.

options.text: Ask the model to restate each timestamp in ISO 8601 in its reasoning before it compares any events
options.explanation: This is still model-side conversion with no guarantee, and it spends tokens on bookkeeping a hook can do exactly.

explanation: Correct: B and C. PostToolUse hooks transform tool results before the model sees them, so heterogeneous timestamps and status codes can be normalised in code. Why not the others: A and E leave conversion to the model, which is probabilistic; D blocks a needed data source instead of normalising its output.
